subtopic: CIVILIAN USE OF LONG BRANCH RIFLE RANGE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. R. O. Campney (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: CIVILIAN USE OF LONG BRANCH RIFLE RANGE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Tuesday last
when the orders of the day were called the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Michener) inquired as to what progress is being made by the Department of National Defence toward making the Long Branch rifle range available for civilian use.
Long Branch rifle range is the only outdoor rifle range operated by the Department of National Defence in the whole Toronto area. It has been so operated for over 40 years. The range serves 17 militia units of battalion or equivalent size, 6 militia units of company size, the regular army troops stationed in the area, personnel of the Royal Canadian Navy and the Royal Canadian Air Force, members of the R.C.M.P. and Ontario provincial and local police, as well as military and other rifle associations.
Use of the range has been increasing steadily throughout the last few years both in numbers of personnel using the range and in time occupied. In 1954 approximately 9,000 personnel shot at the range. The range is therefore of very considerable importance in the field of military training in the Toronto area.
Continuous and very rapid growth of population in the Toronto area during recent years has gradually enveloped the range, and increasing pressure is now being brought to bear on the department to move out. We recognize this situation, but the difficulty has been to find a suitable alternative site. For the past few years we have been making every effort to find an area large enough and close enough to Toronto to develop into a suitable range. We have not met with any success whatever. The whole district around Toronto for many miles is being subdivided and developed, and any prospective site we have found is subject to the same objections which are being directed to our continued occupancy of Long Branch.
On the other hand it must be recognized that the department is obligated to provide shooting facilities for the numerous military units in the Toronto district, either at Long Branch or some other area reasonably accessible to Toronto. In view of the lack of success which is meeting our efforts, we are at present considering the possibilities of Camp Borden which, though 60 miles from Toronto, might, in view of the construction of

a new super highway, serve to meet our military need, though at considerable inconvenience to Toronto units.
In the event that Camp Borden is found practicable, I assume that the lands which we own at Long Branch would be turned over in the usual way to Crown Assets Disposal 'Corporation.
Mr. John Pallet! (Peel): I should like to ask the minister a supplementary question. Was it not the intention of the Department of National Defence to release the Long Branch rifle range by October 1, 1954? If it was the intention to release the range as of that date, what circumstances or what facts have caused the department to alter its original intention?

subtopic: CIVILIAN USE OF LONG BRANCH RIFLE RANGE
speechtext: So far as I know there was never any intention to vacate the Long Branch rifle range by October 1 of last year.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Wednesday, February 2, consideration of the motion of Mr. Yves Leduc (Verdun) for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Rowe, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Hahn.
The Address-Mr. W. M. Hamilton

speakeroldname: Mr. W. M. Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in the course of my remarks yesterday I used the phrase or expression "a government that has the political morality of an alley cat". I notice that in the report in the Gazette this morning, attributed to the Canadian Press, that has been translated and attributed to me as follows: "the morals of an alley cat." I prefer to stand on my original phrase, which restricted it to the political field. The press gallery and the Canadian Press, who are so much better acquainted with the government and have known them so much longer than I have, can make any extension of it they wish.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It might extend to the other side.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You would be included.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
This, Mr. Speaker, is the time of the false prophet. Our progress has been so rapid, the changes around us so great, that many of us have lost sight of those accepted and objective standards by which mankind has been guided for so many generations. This is the age of grotesque and perverse fanaticisms, of bigotries which would be contemptible if they were not all so dangerous. This is the generation of the big lie, the mass delusion. Only the obvious seems not worth saying, only the truth remains in want of publicity. All too often the good is despised as sinful or corrupt and every kind of evil is permitted to parade under the name of virtue.
In this time of change the signs and symbols which have guided the lives of men for centuries have suddenly become unreliable and obscure. In the universal deluge of ideas and mechanical advances men swim about amid the intellectual wreckage of their culture like torpedoed seamen clinging to different coloured bits of straw, not one of them sufficient to support a man.
The cause or occasion of the revolution in our time has been the coming of the machine. But its real challenge, like that of all such periods, is not political or economic so much as it is spiritual. This is the challenge that this government has failed to meet more than any other, the spiritual challenge, the challenge which has brought Canada ever forward. Oh, they have been aided by economic conditions, and they have stayed in power. They have had assistance from various factors, national and international; but as a government and as a party I suggest that they are spiritually gutless and intellectually bankrupt. They have hoped and groped their way through the past 20 years, calling on the civil service for ideas, intelligence and brains.


They have been raiding the same civil service for cabinet material when they could not produce it within their own party. They have been digging into provincial Liberal parties for cabinet material when those same provincial Liberals found they had no future in their own party. '

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: We have never called on you yet.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My
call will come from the people of Canada, not from men who have descended so far that in recent months we have seen them dig into this same civil service, take a man out of it for a preliminary canter in politics, and then when that did not work out put him back into the civil service again. In this respect they treated some of our most cherished traditions of service to this country as they would a box of candy from which you take out one piece, eat it, take out another piece, bite a corner off and put it back into the box.
They have been astute politicians, as leaders they have been lucky; but any government that could produce and support the document which was presented to us a short time ago as the speech from the throne, a document devoid of imagination or of any challenge to the people of this country, a document which refused to accept the facts of economic life in Canada as we find them today, a document which skated around the important issues of the day in order to make reference to matters which are of comparatively minor significance; any party which produces such a document should have nothing but shame in their souls at this point. I for one will vote against any recognition of that document, and without reservations about the party that has brought it into being. I shall be able to do that with great satisfaction.
There are one or two brief points I should like to refer to in passing in case the government has overlooked them. I would remind the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) that the St. Lawrence seaway which is going to have a tremendous effect on our city of Montreal is also well on the way to strangling the traffic passing from the island of Montreal to the south shore. There is one solution and one solution alone which is agreed upon by those who have an intimate knowledge of the situation, and that is a tunnel under the river.
I remind the minister of the need of proper harbour facilities at Montreal, where the passenger sheds are in many ways inferior to our air terminals. You all know what I think of the air terminals of Canada. They bring no credit whatsoever to the great country which

is ours. I would remind the Minister ot Transport of our need for a fireboat at the island.
Finally, I remind the Minister of Transport that Canadians from one coast to the other have hung their heads in shame at the news that the Canadian National Railways has not sufficient trust and confidence in this country to operate their hotel which is being erected with public funds. That is a blot not only on the record of this government but on the record of all Canada. I think the government should look back on this with shame.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon I endeavoured to get leave to discuss a matter of urgent public importance, namely the Formosa situation. I have no criticism to make of the fact that you denied me that request. I think the matter is of urgent public importance, but it is your prerogative to decide whether there is sufficient urgency and whether there is a debate in progress which would permit one to discuss such a matter. This afternoon I want to say something of what I was going to say yesterday.
First 1 want to say I believe that from San Francisco right up to the present time Canada has had many opportunities of speaking out when she has refrained from speaking clearly. I believe that at San Francisco and subsequently Canada was looked upon, because of our situation, because we were not beholden in any way to any other country for the financing of the war or for assistance in our participation in that war, as a country which could speak for that group of nations which is below the level of the five great powers, I do not care whether you call them middle powers or smaller powers.
I am of the opinion that this is the time when Canada should speak with a clear voice regarding the Far Eastern situation. I am going to say that I shall respect the suggestion made yesterday by the acting minister of external affairs, for I am quite certain that what I am going to say this afternoon will create no difficulty or be in any way of an inflammatory nature.
I must confess that I was surprised at the .attitude taken yesterday by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) when he expressed opposition to my request for leave. It is only a few weeks ago' since the hon. member stated that he hoped we were not returning to the days of Mackenzie King, when external affairs were kept more or less under close cover. I might add that I can recollect speeches by the late Gordon Gray-don, when he was spokesman for the Conservative party, and in his absence speeches
The Address-Mr. Coldwell by the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), criticizing the government because time and time again in this house we found ourselves faced with accomplished facts in relation to external affairs.
It seems to me, as I said in my proposed motion yesterday, that this House of Commons should have an opportunity of discussing and expressing an opinion in connection with the grave matters in the Far East. At noon today I heard the one o'clock C.B.C. news broadcast. I regretted exceedingly to hear that the premier of the people's republic of China is refusing the invitation to attend the meeting of the security council, but I understand the reasons for that refusal. It was stated that the premier said he would not be willing to send representatives to the security council until the government on the mainland of China, governing the overwhelming bulk of the Chinese people, was recognized and until the representatives of Chiang Kai-shek were removed both from the United Nations and the security council.
Now, one does not have to agree with the ideology of the government of China to say that that government is in fact the government of China, and has been for several years. Nor does one have to repeat what has been so often repeated in this house, that that government was recognized in 1950 by the government of the United Kingdom, with the expressed public support of the present Prime Minister, Sir Winston Churchill, and the present foreign secretary, Sir Anthony Eden. In other words the British people, through their political leaders of all parties, recognized the fact of a new government in China long ago. So far as this and other countries are concerned, we recognize all kinds of governments, governments that cannot by any stretch of the imagination be classified as democratic and are often totalitarian.
Nor can we hide behind the fact that the government of China came into being through revolution. How often do we recognize the governments of Latin America when constant changes are made in those governments by assassination and by revolution. One can look over the list of the South American governments and see that a number have come into being by revolution and sometimes by assassination, yet we have recognized them. One does not have to agree with the ideology of a government to recognize it as, in fact, the government of a country.
This whole situation regarding Formosa is of course very dangerous, dangerous to the peace of the world; and, should war develop, very dangerous to the security and safety of our own country. It is said, of course, that
798	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Coldwell China's claim to Formosa is based upon insecure grounds. It is said that the claim of the government on the mainland of China to Formosa has failed to recognize the fact that for 50 years Formosa was controlled by Japan, and a century or so before was for 30 years under the government of the Netherlands.
If that is so may I ask, Mr. Speaker, by what right is Chiang Kai-shek there? Chiang Kai-shek says he is the government of China, and claims Formosa on behalf of his regime as the government of China. You cannot have that argument both ways. If Formosa is not in reality a part of China, then why is Chiang Kai-shek there? Why are we recognizing him as the government of China if that is the argument that is used? I heard it used last night by a United States newspaperman speaking from New York during the course of the mid-week review. I say then why is Chiang Kai-shek regarded by us or by anybody else as the government of China if it is true that China has no claim to Formosa?
Of course one cannot overlook the fact that both at Cairo and at Potsdam it was agreed that with the cessation of hostilities Formosa should again become a part of China, as it was before the Japanese conquered it 50 years before. I am not going to say that is the correct disposition of the country. In 1950, when I had the great privilege and pleasure of being associated with our delegation as an observer at the United Nations in New York, I made the suggestion that I thought a proper disposition of Formosa was to neutralize it under the United Nations and let the Formosan people decide what the future of that island should be. I am not arguing that it should be returned to China. I am arguing, hbwever, that the difficulties that have arisen in the Far East, and which now threaten the peace of the world, are largely due to the fact we have failed to recognize that there is a new government in China. We cannot hide behind the argument that that government came into being by revolution or that it has an ideology we do not like. When we look around the world we can see many countries with ideologies we do not like and with governments we do not like, which came into power by revolution.
I want to say, Mr. Speaker, that I believe the policy of the United States in the Far East is just as dangerous, and just as wrong, as I believe the association of Canada with and the strengthening of NATO is right. Just as I believe the one thing, I believe the other.
I believe the one thing because I feel that if we drift along we shall drift into a situation which will bring about a catastrophic war, and I believe the other is a move in the direction of peace. When we look at some of the


statements that have been made recently, such as President Eisenhower's message to congress or the President's news conference of yesterday, we see the dangers that may ensue.
Some of the great newspapers of the world have clearly seen those dangers. Here is a statement by the Manchester Guardian. I do not suppose anyone will say the Manchester Guardian is a socialist newspaper, a communist newspaper or other than what it is, one of the great Liberal newspapers of the world. I have in my hand the issue of January 27, and I should like to read one or two paragraphs from what they say about President Eisenhower's message. They say this:
The ambiguities of President Eisenhower's special-message to congress on Formosa are deplorable. The message is so clumsily constructed that it appears to contain a veiled threat of American attack upon the Chinese mainland. It says that the United States must be prepared to "take appropriate military action" against "any concentration of Chinese communist forces obviously undertaken to facilitate attack upon Formosa."
As I pointed out to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) when he was referring to this particular speech, President Eisenhower failed to say that he would take the same steps to prevent an attack by Chiang's forces on the Chinese mainland. Then after setting forth the situation as they see it, they say this of the speech:
It gives apparent credibility to some of the communist propaganda claiming that the United States is planning an attack upon China. It is a gross blunder.	*
The damaging effect of these phrases cannot be undone by saying that their aim is no more than to assure the security of Formosa and the Pescadores. The threat to the mainland and the implicit American commitment to defend Quemoy remain. It does not help to declaim about "the free world's stake in a free Formosa." Nine-tenths of the free world has grave doubts about, the kind of freedom provided by Chiang's regime (even if it has graver doubts about the communists) .
Those are not my words. Those are the words of the Manchester Guardian. If I may I should like to quote one of our own Canadian papers which has had the respect of a large reading public in Canada over the years, particularly in western Canada. I refer to the Winnipeg Free Press of January 31.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The Address-Mr. Caldwell be made. It cannot be made satisfactorily by force of arms, bringing catastrophe upon the rest of the world.
May I say here I am convinced that what our great neighbour to the south is doing at the present time is alienating the vast millions of people upon whom we must rely in Asia for support in building up democracy all across the world. That is one of the factors in this situation which is most disturbing; the alienation of India, the alienation of Burma, the alienation of Indonesia, the alienation of those teeming millions who look upon the United States as an interloper in a civil war attempting to refasten upon China a form of western imperialism. That is a factor I think we should not overlook, and one reason we should make our position clear while there is yet time. I think the only way this can be done is by negotiations through the United Nations; and if we have to pay the price of recognition of the present government in China, that price is not too high to preserve the peace of the world.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: My hon. friend will realize that it is asked seriously. First, does my friend advocate recognition of the so-called people's government at Peking as the government of the mainland of China and, second, does he advocate that it be recognized as the government of Formosa?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
To the first question I answer yes. I have urged recognition of the people's government of China in this house on a good many occasions over the last several years.
I did not advocate it during the Korean war.
I did advocate it before that war broke out.
I said during the Korean war that as long as that war lasted we could not recognize the people's government of China. The Korean war ended, and I believed there was an opportunity to make that recognition. Earlier in my remarks this afternoon I made it very clear, I believe, that as far as Formosa is concerned it should be placed under the United Nations. It should be neutralized and subsequently the people of Formosa, after the elimination of Chiang and his armies, should decide the future of their own country. That is my position, and I want to make that very clear.
These very negotiations in which we are engaged today do of course involve in effect recognition of China. We negotiated with them directly at Geneva. We negotiated with them on the Korean matter, and it is very difficult to see how you can negotiate 
with a government you do not recognize. If the price we have to pay is recognition, it seems to me that price is well worth paying.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I say I was courteous enough to sit down when the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) rose, but we are not in committee and I do not propose to enter into personal debate. I want to put the view I hold before the house, and if the hon. member disagrees with me I should like to hear his views subsequently.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I just want to ask a question. Mr. Coldwell: All right.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I should like to ask the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) a question in all seriousness, as did the hon. member for Fglinton. The hon. member used the phrase "after Chiang and his army have been eliminated from Formosa". What did he mean by that?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I did not mean elimination by war. If the island were placed under the United Nations I think the United Nations would of course eliminate Chiang as the ruler and governor of Formosa. That is what I mean, to eliminate him as the governor and government of Formosa.
I said that the very negotiations we have undertaken from time to time have involved recognition, and I say that Canada should speak up today because other nations look to us to speak on some of these matters, and we have not always done so. I should like to refer to a statement of the leader of the opposition in Great Britain, and in this regard I am certain that he is speaking for more than the people within his own party.
I have here an Associated Press dispatch from London, dated January 31, reading in part as follows:
Clement R. Attlee, leader of Britain's Labour party, declared today that Chiang Kai-shek and his top nationalist officials should be exiled from Formosa.
That is one step beyond what I suggested a moment ago. It would seem to be quite necessary to do that. The dispatch continues: The island's people should then decide by plebiscite whether they want to join red China, Attlee said in a copyright interview in the Labour newspaper, Daily Herald.
I may say I am not following Mr. Attlee here, because I made this suggestion in 1950 when I was associated with the Canadian delegation at New York.
In any case, the United States should drop forthwith the claim that Formosa is part of its Pacific defence ring.

"I cannot see myself that the island of Formosa is an essential part of the defence of the United States of America in this era of the hydrogen bomb", Attlee said.
"It is clear that the Peiping government won the civil war against Chiang Kai-shek. It would then have occupied Formosa but for the intervention of the United States fleet. The American action taken at the same time as the United Nations action in Korea, in 1950, had nothing to do with the United Nations but was dictated by an American policy of security."
As I indicated earlier, the Secretary of State for External Affairs made it abundantly clear in the house at that time that we were in no way involved in that particular policy. I continue:
"Since that time the forces of Chiang Kai-shek have constantly attacked the Chinese mainland. It seems to me quite unreasonable that under the shelter of American forces the Chiang party should be able to carry on a civil war."
I think that sums up the situation very well. I do not want to say much more, Mr. Speaker. I think I have made my point. The point I am making is that Canada at this time should make it very clear where we stand. I should have liked to see the house yesterday support the statement made here on January 25 by the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I do not expect, of course, that the minister, conducting the external affairs of this country, could rise in his place and say all that I have said this afternoon, but I am in a somewhat different position. I am not responsible for the conduct of external affairs, but I am responsible for expressing the views of what I believe to be a very large section of the Canadian people and, more than that, a very large section of public opinion throughout the democratic world.
I think I have quoted sufficiently this afternoon. I could have quoted the London Times and other papers to the same effect but, because we have a Liberal government in power in Canada, I chose to quote from a good British Liberal newspaper, the Manchester Guardian, and from the Winnipeg Free Press, which is an equally well known Liberal paper in our country.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I express my wholehearted support of what the Secretary of State for External Affairs said in the house on January 25 in dealing with this particular aspect of international affairs, and plead with our government to use its influence to see to it that a peaceful settlement of the trouble in the Formosa area is negotiated. If the price we have to pay is recognition of a fact, recognition that a government does exist on the mainland of China-even though, as I said, it exists like so many other governments, 50433-51

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) said there was a difference between the role which he plays on that side of the house and the role of the spokesman for the government in the matter of foreign affairs at this time. That affords me the opportunity of saying that he will not misunderstand if I confine myself, in the brief observations I wish to make today, to the basic question he has put this afternoon, and which he mentioned on two occasions yesterday when he intervened in the deliberations of the house.
The government of Canada is anxious that all possible steps should be taken to stop the fighting in the Formosa strait; and it is because of that consideration that I do not want now to say anything that might interfere with important negotiations now going on. I can only reiterate with even greater confidence than yesterday the wisdom of the course suggested for us in the House of Commons at this time. At the moment the security council of the United Nations has this question before it, but discussions have been adjourned pending a reply to the invitation to the communist Chinese government to attend the council sessions.
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar said he had heard over the radio at noon that a reply in the negative had come from the so-called Chinese people's republic. By telephone and subsequently by wire, I have been in touch with our ambassador, the permanent delegate at the United Nations, and as a result

The Address-Mr. Martin I am not in a position to give an unqualified statement as to the nature of the reply that is now, I understand, on its way to the Secretary General of the United Nations. From what has been sent to me in the house, since I have entered the chamber, I would not be justified in making any comment as to the nature of this reply.
I think the situation at the moment is such that in any event one could characterize the news services account as not justifying final observation. Notwithstanding that, undoubtedly, whatever be the nature of the communist reply, the security council, which has adjourned its session to await the reply, will be convoked within the next day or so, and consideration will be given by that body to what course should be followed. I would hope that the security council will still find it possible-I know they will find it desirable -not to lose control of this matter.
Canada is not of course a member of the security council; but our ambassador, the permanent delegate there, is following the deliberations of the council closely, and is in constant touch with its members. The security council has had success in the past in a mediatory or good offices role and we hope, as I am sure all members in the house hope, that it will be able to bring about a cease-fire in this instance, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out last Friday it has done in a number of other instances.
Meanwhile the prime ministers of the commonwealth countries who have gathered in London have obviously been preoccupied to some extent with the Formosa situation. I have had the opportunity of learning the nature of their discussions, but the house would not expect me at this time to make any further observations about the full character and scope of those discussions, except perhaps to say that there have been some general exchanges of views on the subject at the meetings of the prime ministers. It is not the normal practice at conferences of commonwealth prime ministers to take decisions on questions like this. There have also been some informal discussions among those attending the conference, directed to the same objective as that of the security council, namely the stopping of the fighting.
The view of the Canadian government during the Korean hostilities was that Formosa should be neutralized. This idea of the neutralization of Formosa is still applicable in the present situation. As the hon. member who has just spoken pointed out, the government's view was stated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on January 25.

Yesterday the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar made this observation:
Mr. Speaker, may I just add that the occasion for seeking leave to discuss this matter is that news from London today indicates that a position differing from that taken by our government on January 25 is being taken by our representatives at the commonwealth conference in London.
Later he reiterated this observation, when he said:
My request is based entirely upon what was said by the Secretary of State for External Affairs in the house on January 25 and the fact that authoritative statements from London today indicate that there has been a change of attitude by our representatives there.
On January 25 my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs said this in the house:
Pending such a decision-
That is, a settlement about the future of Formosa.
-I think that a strong case can be made for the neutralization of Formosa both in order to prevent any assault upon it by communist forces and also so that it will not be used as a base for invasion of the mainland.
I have read carefully the other observations of the Secretary of State for External Affairs and the text of the speech which last Friday night he made over the network of the national broadcasting system. I think I may say that what he said, in substance, was as follows. A clear distinction must be made between Formosa and the Pescadores and the small islands along the Chinese coast. Formosa and the Pescadores have not been part of the territory of China for a good many years, and their present status is not very clear. The small islands along the coast are, however, indisputably Chinese territory. The views on neutralization expressed in this way do not necessarily apply to the coastal islands. Because of these circumstances it would be a great disaster if incidents in the small coastal islands were to lead to a general war.
These are not my colleague's actual words, but rather my paraphrasing of them. And he went on-again paraphrasing what he said- what is needed at the moment is to stop the fighting, without prejudice to the claims of either side or to an eventual political settlement. If this can be brought about and if the Chinese nationalist forces now on the coastal islands can be withdrawn, the resulting truce might go on for some years, as have similar truces in other parts of the world. In the resulting atmosphere a more permanent settlement might be reached by negotiation or perhaps by an international conference. Such a settlement should, of course, take into account the wishes of the inhabitants of Formosa.

The action which the United States government has taken in the Formosa area does not commit Canada or other countries. Any obligation we might have in regard to the Formosa strait could arise only from our responsibility as a member of the United Nations. Although we are not committed by United States policies, we are certainly affected by them. That is why we welcome the assurances which President Eisenhower gave on January 27 that the United States forces in the Formosa area would be used purely for defensive purposes. We are confident that the United States government will exercise a moderating, influence also on the Chinese nationalist government. In connection with the mutual defence treaty which the two governments signed, there was an exchange of notes between Mr. Dulles and Mr. Yeh, the foreign minister of the republic of China, on December 10. These notes provided that the use of force in the treaty area by either power would be a matter of joint agreement except for self-defence in an emergency.
I can assure the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar and the house that the policy of the Canadian government concerning the Formosa situation has not departed in any way from the principles laid down in the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs in this house on January 25, and again in the statement he made over the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation network last Friday. So there can be no doubt about that, I quote now directly from a communication that I have had from the Secretary of State for External Affairs in London, who is there associated with the Prime Minister at this time. His message to me is as follows:
There is no foundation at all to any report or suggestion that in regard to Formosa the Canadian policy has departed in any way from the principles laid down in my statement to the house on January 25 and in my broadcast of last Friday.

In order to bring the attention of the house back to the discussion which was proceeding yesterday may I read the amendment moved by the Social Credit party during the speech of the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn)? It is as follows:
We further regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to take or to recommend the necessary fundamental economic and financial measures to place Canadian producers and workers on a sound and prosperous basis, and to ensure our economy against recurring recessions.
I have read that, Mr. Speaker, because I want you to know that I am going to phrase 50433-511
The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston my remarks as carefully as I can in order to follow the wording of the amendment.
One of the most important problems that faced Canada last year, the year before that and the year preceding that, was the distressing position in which agriculture found itself. That is important to us as a nation. It is important to us as members of this house because the prosperity of Canada depends directly upon the prosperity of our agricultural industry. That is only natural when one remembers that agriculture is the basic industry of Canada. Despite the progress we have made in other lines, agriculture still remains of prime importance.
Agriculture is a big industry. Because that is so it is necessary that we give it due consideration. It is so important that anything which affects agriculture directly affects all other industry in this country. We experienced that last year. It has become more noticeable because of increasing unemployment. Farmers were not able to buy; therefore industry felt a slackening off in business and as a result, we are heading for an economic depression, or some might prefer to call it a recession.
There is growing concern among the farmers not because agriculture has failed-it has not-but because of accumulating surpluses. To me, Mr. Speaker, that is not a reason to become panicky; in. fact we should rejoice that Providence has permitted us to have surpluses. If we are in such an economic position that we do not know what to do with our surpluses, surely we cannot blame the good Lord for that. We must accept our own ignorance as being to blame. To me the matter of surpluses has always been something of which we should be proud. I have always taken the stand, and have so expressed myself in this house on other occasions, that what we should have in Canada is sufficient storage capacity so that we could have our supplies stored in, as I call it, an ever-ready granary, one that we could call upon in time of emergency.
It has been the experience of those of us who have lived in this country for any length of time that over a period of time nature pretty well takes care of any surplus. The surpluses we have on hand now would not be more than sufficient to take care of our needs if we were to have a crop failure or, certainly if we were to have two crop failures. Under those conditions we might find ourselves in very difficult straits. Therefore, because we have a surplus we should not become panicky. The thing that is disturbing to the agriculturists is that they have no money. I would not assume that we can blame anybody else but ourselves. We have

The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston fallen down in this house as legislators in our endeavour to provide sufficient money, which is the means of distribution. Of course, everybody in the country is looking to us or more properly to this government for a solution.
I said a moment ago that when we have adverses in agriculture they are reflected in all the industries in this country. The cash registers stop ringing and we have disasters in industry. We have found that condition in the smaller industries. It is now taking place in the larger industries. Last year retail sales in this country have fallen by over $260 million. They fell by a similar amount in 1953, and we shall find that they will fall a greater amount in 1955 unless our policies are changed.
There is another indication that this will take place; that is the tremendous increase in credit buying. One has only to pick up the newspapers to find that industry is trying to develop all sorts of ingenious ways to get people to buy beyond their means, even to the extent of forfeiting their future pay. I noticed in the paper the other day that a television set was offered by a firm in this town. They had what I thought was a rather clever way of getting people to pledge their future earnings. They agreed to put this television set in a person's house without any down payment. On the machine was a money meter, and every time the person used that television set they would put 50 or 75 cents in the meter. At the end of the month the agent would come along and collect the money for the month's payment. That was a rather ingenious form of credit selling.
If we could put an equal amount of energy into trying to find an economic solution to this problem I am sure we would reach some solution. In connection with credit buying I should like to refer to an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of January 7. It is rather long, and I shall read only two short paragraphs as follows:
Consumer Credit at All-Time High of $1,885,000,000
The amount of money Canadians owe for the things they buy on credit has reached an all-time high.
The Bank of Canada estimates the outstanding consumer credit bill rose to a record $1,885,000,000 at September 30 last, an increase of $19,000,000 from the previous quarter and a jump of more than $100,000,000 from the previous year.
If we follow the same trend it will not take much imagination to see what is going to happen to our business concerns. In 1954 there was a total of $1,885 million of credit buying, which does not take into consideration any of the money loaned through the

farm loan board or under the National Housing Act. If those amounts are added you have a colossal amount of credit buying. It seems to me that should be sufficient warning for us to encourage, even to demand, that this government take drastic steps in order to make it possible for the farmers to realize something as a result of their labour. These are forerunners of disaster which cannot be denied.
If we look at the farm income for 1954 we find that it was $2,408,600,000. Things are not improving. We must recognize that in 1954 there was an income drop of over $300 million. That was the estimate given in a report to the federal-provincial agriculture conference held not long ago. In

If we recognize that agriculture is the basic industry of this country it takes no stretch of the imagination to see what is going to happen unless something is done.
I suggested a moment ago that any slackening off in the income of agriculture will be reflected in business conditions in this country. I have in my hand the Monetary Times of December, 1954, a very reliable financial paper, and speaking on this matter they say:
The rate of business failures in Canada is continuing its post-war rise, but still has a long way to go to match pre-war figures, it is indicated in Dun and Bradstreet's report for the first nine months of this year. Up 42 per cent from 1953 figures, failures in the first three quarters of

This would seem to indicate that bigger firms with greater liabilities are being involved, suggesting the shake-out of smaller businesses has been completed.
It would seem to be clear from that report that small businesses have already collapsed, and now the axe is about to fall on some of the larger businesses in this country. Surely these signs cannot be ignored, and the government is bound to take these matters into consideration.

It certainly was scandalous. I did not hear the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) criticize that

It should be remembered, Mr. Speaker-and I do not recall the hon. member for Kootenay East giving us these facts-that when the Canadian Pacific undertook to build that railroad they were given a subsidy of $3,404,720. Then as a further subsidy to offset any losses which might occur they were given 250,000 acres of land, together with the oil and mineral rights. The oil and mineral rights alone have amounted to millions of dollars, and there is no saying how many more millions the company will derive from that property as the result of that gift.
It should not be forgotten, either, that only a year or so ago this government gave the railways a subsidy of $7 million a year to compensate them for any loss in handling freight north of the great lakes. In all, I feel it can be fairly said that the railways of this country have been very generously treated. In fact they have been so generously treated and their revenues are up so well-if you consider all the revenues which they receive from their different enterprises-that they do not need to interfere now nor at any time with this Crowsnest pass agreement. I am in hopes that the new Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) will not be as easily influenced by railway propaganda as was the last minister of transport.
Speaking in this house about a year and a half ago I made a prediction, Mr. Speaker, and I feel I should draw it to your attention now. I never claimed to be a prophet, but this prophecy came true. I said then that the minister of transport was going to be relieved of his job and given a greater reward; and that has come to pass. He is now chairman of the St. Lawrence seaway authority. I am not questioning his ability to fill that position at all. I say without fear of contradiction that he was one of the best supporters the Canadian Pacific and Canadian National had in this country. It did not seem to matter whether or not the interests of the ordinary man were in the way.
I should like to refer to another aspect of agriculture, and to the way in which I feel this government may be able to be of some assistance. I believe we should have a definite support price for agricultural products, not because of any situation in which we find ourselves right now, although that would be sufficient argument, but because this government promised such support to the farmers of this country. We all recall quite well that during the war the government agreed to see to it that the farmers would not lose in the long run because they were forced to take

The Address-Mr. C. E. Johnston controlled prices at that time. It is well known that because of the controlled prices of agricultural products in Canada during the war, particularly wheat, Great Britain was able to give her people cheap bread. It will be recalled that during the same period western agriculturists were once again asked to finance low cost bread for our own Canadian people. This is the only instance of which I am aware where one particular industry in a nation was asked to subsidize low cost living for the rest of the people in that country.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) assured the farmers of this nation that they would not lose because of that. It is only right, therefore, that the government should honour that pledge and institute a complete policy of agricultural prices support. It is true that shortly afterward the farmers were given $65 million to compensate them for a loss of $350 million. It must not be forgotten, either, that there was quite a debate at that time, and it was the Conservative party that refused to vote that $65 million for the agriculturists of western Canada.
Then, too, I believe the government should approve the suggestion made here last year by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), which took the form of a resolution in these words:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration the advisability of enacting legislation at this session of parliament to provide for a system of approved farm storage under which the wheat board may make advances to farmers on grain held on the farm.
As I said a moment ago, the situation in which the farmers find themselves is not the result of too much grain but is the result of the fact they have not received the money for the grain they have grown. I recognize immediately that there has been some difficulty in the sale of that wheat. There should be no difficulty, however, in the way of the government making advances to farmers for grain in approved storage on the farms. I would go so far as to say that the government itself should make these advances through the Bank of Canada, perhaps with the assistance of the wheat board. If the government took advantage of this suggestion they could certainly give the farmers loans at a very low rate of interest.
I feel, too, that the government could make quite a few tax cuts in order to give the farmers and others some relief. The taxes being extracted from the consuming public of this country put the people in a position where they can no longer buy the goods that are being produced. This is affecting not only agriculture but all the other industries in this country. I would suggest


that the income tax exemption should be set at $1,500 for single persons and at least $3,000 for married persons. The government might consider als6 the elimination, in part at least, of the exorbitant excise and sales taxes now being imposed upon the people of this country.
Let me turn my attention for a few moments to another aspect of the matter which needs some consideration. I am still dealing precisely with the amendment which I read a moment ago, Mr. Speaker. I want to say a word or two about the unemployment problem. This question has been dealt with before, but I feel it needs repeating. In the speech from the throne the government made reference to unemployment as being of a regional and seasonal nature. Of course we all know that the government was somewhat ill-informed on that occasion, because neither then nor now could unemployment be termed regional or seasonal. Even if it were, it would be so important that this government should take some steps to see to it that no one was in dire need in a country with such vast wealth as we have. It was not so long ago that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made a plea to labour to knuckle down and produce more. They did that with such efficiency that they have now produced themselves into the soup kitchens. They have been producing so much that industry cannot sell it, and as a result they have had to lay off men. These men are now unemployed.
It is well to remember that 75 per cent of the people of this country are earning less than $3,000 a year. In the light of that fact we can readily understand why the standard of living of the majority of the people of this country is not too high. I am not exaggerating when I say that at least 50 per cent of the people of this country are living on less than $2,000 a year, and that is pretty low.
We realize that their standard of living is not too high. There is only one reason the people of this country do not have a higher standard of living. It is that they have not the purchasing power with which to buy the goods they desire. It is not a case of getting more jobs. It is not a case of what the Prime Minister said a year or so ago, "Get out, work harder and produce more". They have worked so hard that they have worked themselves right out of a job. Surely that is an economic fact that even the most elementary student can grasp.

In the thirties I think the figure for those registered and others was about half a million. But it should be pointed out again that these people are unemployed during a time of so-called prosperity. As the welfare council points out, the number does not make any difference; if there is only one unemployed person in this country who is destitute something should be done in order to see that that family does not suffer. Particularly is that true, Mr. Speaker, when we have in this country so many goods that we cannot dispose of. When we have a surplus of almost everything, nobody should be in want.
From what I have pointed out to you, Mr. Speaker, it would seem clear that this country is in need of increased purchasing power. I am not at the moment going to enter into an argument as to the way in which that increased purchasing power can be obtained. Social Credit have what they believe to be the solution for the difficulty, but they are not the ones who are burdened with the responsibility of seeing that purchasing power is put in the hands of the people to buy the things that are being produced and that cannot be sold. That is the responsibility of the government. If they cannot discharge that responsibility, then in due course the people will have to take what action they deem to be necessary.
It should be clear that whenever there is this economic downtrend, the government needs some sort of mechanism in their policy which would put purchasing power in the hands of the people, and that purchasing power should become effective demand, so the people can buy the goods which are being made but which cannot be sold. How they are going to do that is their business; but it should be understood-and I do not think anybody will contradict this statement-that the act of buying makes jobs. Whenever you get the public in the position where they cannot buy, then you just cannot give jobs. When industry cannot sell the goods they are producing, then of course industry must close.
In my judgment it is not proper to blame private enterprise for the unemployment we have amongst us today, because private enterprise has excelled itself. It has so excelled


itself that it is producing goods that cannot be sold. Therefore it must let the men go. Even the labour unions themselves recognize that fact. Let me refer to the Canadian Congress of Labour submission to the government on November 12, 1954, when they had this to say at page 4:
What we ought to do is put money into the hands of people who will buy what we can already make and can't sell.
That is the crux of the situation. It is up to the government to see that that is done.
There are other matters I should have liked to talk about today. I wanted to speak about the coal industry, an industry that is indeed sick and needs something done about it. Their difficulties should not be shrugged aside as the minister did a year or so ago, when he said he knew that the coal mining industry was in a bad position but that it would do them good to have a little squeeze. Well, they are certainly being squeezed. If that was the solution they should now be on the road to recovery, but unfortunately that was not the solution. I want to speak about coal but I cannot do so on this occasion because my time will not permit.
On another occasion-and I shall take advantage of my privileges in this house to do so-I want to speak about one of our greatest national parks in Canada, not one of the greatest but the greatest as statistics will indicate; that is, Banff national park. I want to speak about how the government has neglected to do what should have been done for the greatest national park in Canada. I shall take advantage of the privileges that are mine in this house on another occasion, and I shall continue to put forward arguments for both these interests.

As a young Canadian with little experience in the House of Commons I was sorry to hear some of the comments uttered by members of the C.C.F. party, for I was brought up and educated by people who taught me all along to love my fellow citizens of British Columbia just as well as my fellow citizens of the maritime provinces. I will now speak of shipping, and of some of the related problems in the hope of bringing about some change in the present situation.
I shall not deal today at length with the complex and difficult problem of deciding whether Canada should have a sea-going merchant navy, but I shall limit myself to coastal shipping on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence.
The Address-Mr. Maltais
Nobody can deny the vital part played by water transport in a country in the geographical position of Canada, whose limits extend as far west as the Pacific ocean, north to the Arctic ocean and east to the Atlantic ocean. In addition, it is connected with the latter ocean by a waterway extending over some 2,000 miles, if we include 'the great lakes, along which are located, more particularly from Montreal to Port Arthur, the greatest industrial centres of the country.
That long waterway has undoubtedly been the main factor in Canada's economic development and it continues to facilitate the unprecedented industrial expansion we have seen for some years past. It is rather difficult to assess in terms of dollars and cents the volume of products shipped by water, from the great lakes to various points on the St. Lawrence and outside the country, but a fair idea of the importance of that waterway can be gathered from the fact that more ships pass through the Sault Ste. Marie canals in seven months than through the Suez canal in a whole year.
According to the statistics I have obtained, more than 200 million tons of goods were shipped through that waterway in 1953. From a further breakdown of the statistics, showing a comparison between the present volume of traffic and that of preceding years, it appears that the shipping activity on the St. Lawrence gives a good idea of our country's economy.
In 1932, at the worst of the depression, only 3-5 million tons of ore were shipped through that waterway, while in 1953 nearly 95 million tons passed through it.
Although it is hard to get exact percentages regarding the nature of the products usually shipped, certain facts indicate that the tonnage of goods shipped may be divided as follows: grain comes first among the goods shipped, accounting for 36 per cent of the total; then oil and related products, with approximately 19 per cent. Pulp wood accounts for 8 per cent, coal 6 per cent, lumber in general, except pulpwood, 4-5 per cent and iron ore, about 2 [DOT] 5 per cent.
Those few figures pertaining exclusively to water transport on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence give us a good idea of the importance of coastal shipping for the economy of our country, and give us an insight into the expansion that will follow the deepening of the St. Lawrence and into the developments it will mean for the north shore.
810

The Address-Mr. Maltais
Not only will that activity of Canadian shipping in the vital field of transport increase the number of ships sailing on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence shipping but it is part of a national industry made up of skilled labour, experienced crews, technical apparatus, shipyards and tremendous capital investments.
It is therefore not surprising, Mr. Speaker, that the seamen of my constituency, situated on the north shore of the St. Lawrence, have expressed their fears and apprehension at the difficulties which seem to be increasing as a result of our legislation and of international agreements. The deepening of the St. Lawrence, which is now underway, will open up the whole great lakes district to unlimited shipping and will give access to the most industrialized part of the country. That is why Canada's merchant marine is getting more and more apprehensive, and the position of our ship owners will become unbearable unless more adequate measures are taken to help them.
The shipping act of 1934 contains nearly all the necessary provisions for the protection, control and regulation of Canadian ships. Certain international conventions, to which we have become a party, supplement that legislation. I do not hesitate to say that much of the trouble now experienced by our merchant marine results from the legal freedom enjoyed by the British merchant marine under the 1931 convention pertaining to the British commonwealth merchant marine, to compete here in Canada with our own ships for the transportation of goods.
At present, ships of all nations have access to the navigation facilities of the St. Lawrence, as far as the great lakes, but Canadian coastal trade is exclusively reserved to ships of British and Canadian registry.
Thus a ship built in Great Britain and flying the British flag can engage in coastal trade in Canadian inland waters. In other words, that ship may carry goods from port to port within Canada. This freedom of the British merchant marine to engage in coastal trade in our home waters is such as to place our own inland waters shipping in a difficult position. I am not speaking here of our high seas merchant fleet, since it is now practically non-existent. When a British seaman receives a monthly salary of $80 as against $200 for the Canadian seaman in a similar occupation, it is easy to understand the kind of unfair competition which any ship flying

the Canadian flag has to face from her British competitor. Besides, any British built ship is far cheaper to build and repair in British yards where salaries are again far lower than our own. This also adds substantially to the operating costs of a Canadian vessel as against that of a British vessel where the wage scale is far below that of the competing country.
Due to such low operating costs, several small ships of British registry are now plying the St. Lawrence river, and the competition our smaller shipping companies have to put up with in that respect is unfair, because they cannot carry that freight at the same rate.
We are now earmarking millions of dollars for the St. Lawrence seaway so that ocean shipping might more easily reach the great lakes. That project enables us to foresee still greater opportunities for our coastal shipping, and we know already that British ship owners are seriously considering an increase in the competition that we have to meet from their ships along the large seaway that the St. Lawrence river will be a few years from now.
Not later than last year, the inland shipping trade of Canada lost to British ships part of the transport resulting from hydroelectric power developments on the north shore of the river, with the help of Canadian capital.
If this situation is allowed to continue, the sacrifices made by the people of Canada in developing the world's longest seaway within our country will have served to dig the graveyard of what is left of the Canadian merchant marine.
Consequently, I ask the government that governments of all other parts of the British commonwealth of nations be notified with the least possible delay, and under article 24, part X of the convention, that Canada intends to amend the terms of the convention relating to the merchant marine of the British commonwealth and establish certain requirements regarding all coastal trade carried out in Canadian waters by any ship of other than Canadian registry.
Australia and New Zealand have already taken steps to protect their respective coastal trade by providing that foreign vessels would have to pay their crews salary rates in accordance with those already in force in their country, with the result that Australian coastal trade is practically limited to Australian ships.
The United States goes further by limiting that trade to truly American ships, built and registered in the United States.

Besides, our merchant shipping is the only-industry to face such unfair competition.
Our aviation is fully protected, and Canada was one of the first nations at the Chicago convention in 1944 to provide for the introduction of section 7 entitled "coastal navigation" and accepted at the international civil aviation convention.
This clause reads as follows:
Each contracting state may refuse to allow an aircraft of another contracting state to pick up passengers or cargo within its own territory and to carry them on a paying basis to another point of this territory.
The clause goes even further, by forbidding any contracting state to make arrangements or conclude treaties with another state, when the advantages and benefits allowed under the agreement are not shared by the other countries on the same basis.
Mr. Speaker, if it were possible to protect Canadian airlines, I fail to understand why our merchant marine could not also be given protection in the best interests of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the first subject I wish to discuss this afternoon is the need for cabinet representation in that great industrial belt extending from Chatham on the west to Cornwall on the east, then northward for 50 miles from the St. Lawrence river, lake Ontario and the United States boundary.
In reality this area is the heartland of Canadian industry. In it live about three million people, which is about one-fifth of the total population of Canada. Yet there is no cabinet representation for this vast and important area of our country. It is an area that needs representation so that the problems of industry can be brought before the cabinet continuously, and so that the cabinet may be made constantly aware of the problems which industry and those who work in it are facing.
Had that been the case, I am confident the government would not have been making the attempts it is now making to brush off as something merely seasonal and regional the unemployment situation which, last year, month by month averaged 70 per cent more than in the corresponding months of the year before. I make this statement from figures supplied by the minister's department which I have checked and know to be correct.
If this great industrial area was represented in cabinet discussions I believe there is a good chance that the government would be far more inclined than it is today to consider reducing the high commodity taxes many of 50433-52i
The Address-Mr. Hees our goods are carrying; taxes which are helping to price many Canadian goods out of both the domestic and export markets.
I believe there is a very good chance that if this area was represented by a minister who, because of his location in the area and his connection with its industry, was familiar with the problems of industry and the people who work in it, he would be able to explain to his colleagues that the cutting of commodity taxes does not necessarily mean a reduction in tax revenues.
The reduction of commodity taxes makes it possible to sell more goods; and if the correct balance can be struck, the total tax revenue may easily be greater when commodity taxes are reduced than at a time when high taxes are stifling the sale of products, as we see today.
A very good example of that was given to the government a while ago when they foolishly, and over our objections, raised the tax on cigarettes. The minister of finance found that when the tax rose, a lot of people stopped smoking cigarettes, and the sales fell off so badly that the total tax revenue was reduced considerably below what it had been when the tax was lower. The government had to reduce the tax to where it had been before. The sales of cigarettes picked up, and the total tax revenue went back to the higher figure, a figure considerably higher than when the tax was raised.
With that example before us, I hope the government will give consideration to reducing many of our high commodity taxes, because they are playing a very important part in pricing goods out of the market and making it impossible for many of our workmen to work full time. Often those workmen are laid off completely, and that is one of the main causes of the serious unemployment situation which exists, but which the government refuses to face in its true reality today.
Another thing that happens when you reduce commodity taxes is that more goods are sold. You have more people working and earning an income on which they pay an income tax to the government, instead of drawing on the government for unemployment insurance benefits when they are unemployed. Mr. Speaker, there is a lot of plain straight arithmetic which this government has to consider because of the serious situation existing in our economy today. They have to stop pretending the situation does not exist; they have to stop brushing unemployment aside as seasonal and regional, and face the facts and examine this whole problem as an economic one and not as a political one which should be dodged and ducked. This

The Address-Mr. Hees government owes it to the country to face the facts and come up with concrete, constructive and economically sound plans for getting at and curing the basic causes of unemployment and lost markets.
It seems strange to me that with the many Liberal members in the house who live in the area that I have described, it is impossible for the Prime Minister to find one whom he considers capable of holding down a cabinet post. When we form a government we shall have no trouble at all forming an excellent cabinet to run the country far better than this government is running it. It seems strange that the Prime Minister is having this difficulty in picking a cabinet minister to represent an area which is, as I say, the heartland of Canadian industry.
In that area about one-fifth of the total population of Canada live. There is one member in this house who, as hon. members know, has had the experience of being the mayor of one of our large industrial cities. He has had the experience of being a cabinet minister in a Liberal provincial government of one of our large provinces. He has been the chairman of the defence expenditure committee, and is now the chairman of the banking and commerce committee, the most important committee of this house. I ask the Prime Minister-I wish he were here, but I hope he will give us an answer when he comes back-why it is, if he considers a member good enough for such important positions as I have just outlined, he is not capable of holding down a position in the cabinet.
In refusing to appoint a cabinet minister from inside this house, as the Prime Minister has done twice within a year, he has in effect said to the 150 members of his party who are not in the cabinet:	You just do
not have the ability to sit in my cabinet and I must go outside and choose a minister from outside of parliament. In effect he has said to them: I cannot have confidence in you. And twice, as has been said today, he has had to go outside. I think it is a pity.
