appreciate the fact, Mr. Speaker, that under the procedure of this house an hon. member may speak more than once during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Officially, of course, we are now discussing the subamendment moved by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Hahn). Unofficially, of course, we can speak on any matter that comes to our mind. However, because we are officially discussing the subamendment I want to say that I have listened with a great deal of interest to the 

remarks of the hon. member for New Westminster. I have read with a great deal of interest and studied the amendment that he moved. I am, therefore, going to vote for it. I cannot do anything else.
The subamendment could be put in this way. Are you in favour of better weather in Ottawa? I certainly am. Now, economically and politically, that is the meaning of the amendment moved by the hon. member. I would say the amendment is one that you cannot vote against. It is something indefinite. I am going to vote for it because if those principles were put into effect there might be some improvement. It is in no way specific in its terms. My friend on my right says, "according to his ideas." Socred ideas are not specific in the amendment. The wording is general and that was known when the amendment was moved.
I want to speak on three points this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, two of which have been already mentioned. Although these two have been raised, I feel it is important that those who support these two suggestions make their position known, because if only one person speaks perhaps no attention will be paid to him. First of all, I want to speak on a matter that was mentioned in this debate and this afternoon was the subject of questions, that is the financial contribution of the federal government to a bridge over the north arm of the Fraser river. It has become known as the Marpole bridge, but actually that is a misnomer. I cannot understand the position of the federal government on this issue.
On going over the records I find that on October 15, 1946, a committee was appointed to examine into the question of a' bridge in that area. The committee was composed of seven engineers, including two dominion government engineers, and had representatives from the city of Vancouver and province of British Columbia as well. On November 14, 1947, this committee, which I repeat included two dominion government engineers, made a report recommending a new bridge but not at the present location of the Mar-pole bridge. There have been developments and negotiations since 1946. I, personally, was a member at some of the conferences held, at which at least one of our present cabinet ministers was present. We were given to understand that we would be assisted.
I have been reading with a great deal of interest some of the statements that have emanated from the Department of Public Works in Ottawa during the past few months. They are very contradictory. They would lead one to believe that the government had no idea of the plans for the bridge, and that

no application was made by the British Columbia government for financial assistance.
I was interested in this matter, so before I came to Ottawa I went to Victoria. I found that on March 25 of last year the Department of Public Works was sent all the plans of the proposed new bridge. I found also that on May 11 a letter was sent to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters) requesting federal assistance up to one-third of the cost of that bridge. I am sorry that the Minister of Public Works is not in his seat, for I have on my desk a copy of the report of the 1946 committee as well as a record of the letters sent by the provincial government in March and in May.
What I am trying to do, sir, is to continue the remarks I made when I spoke first in this debate to the effect that the federal government has a responsibility for the major highways, byways and bridges in a province. There can be no question but that this bridge is required. There can be no question but that it serves one of the major international airports of the dominion. In view of the present international crisis, there can be no question but that the major international airport is Vancouver. Along with other members of parliament from all parties, I attended a meeting of the airport committee in Vancouver prior to the calling of this session. We were told that under no circumstances would the R.C.A.F. recede from its position that the Sea island airport was the station for the R.C.A.F. Therefore from the point of view of a highway proposition, a defence proposition and an R.C.A.F. proposition there is a major interest on the part of the federal government in the existence of proper access to that international airport. I just want to add my words to those that have already been spoken, and to the questions that were asked only this afternoon on the orders of the day, urging that the federal government reconsider its position and, in the light of all the circumstances, make a major contribution to the cost of this $10 million new bridge which is now almost under construction, or at least for which tenders have already been called.
There is one other point I wish to make. Unless the federal government does so Vancouver, the third city of Canada, will again be hemmed in by toll bridges. I am not going to say any more on that matter. I spoke on it last session and I am just adding my words to those which have been spoken on it at this session.
On my second point, I again am only adding my voice to those of other hon. members who spoke at this present session asking the federal government to reconsider its policy
The Address-Mr. Winch on the age limit of those who can get a government job. I admit that I am now rapidly approaching the age of 50. Nevertheless, at least my constituents think that I have not reached a point where I am past the age where I can be a member of the House of Commons. Yet, Mr. Speaker, there is no question whatsoever that throughout Canada in industry there is a growing requirement to the effect that you cannot get a job if you are over 45, and unfortunately now it is over 40. I understand there is a similar regulation with respect to employment by the federal government.
I believe that the Vancouver Daily Province under date of January 14 had a most interesting editorial which I should like to quote in part. It draws our attention to the fact that in British Columbia-which I think I can safely say is one of the most rapidly growing provinces of the Dominion of Canada and has perhaps the greatest potentialities for future development-in the past few weeks it has been found necessary to form a brand new organization. That organization is being called "Experienced Employables over 40".
This is the first time that I have discussed this matter on the floor of the House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, but it was my privilege to discuss it more than once in the British Columbia legislature. I should like to repeat what I said a number of years ago, and what I still believe to be true, namely that it is wrong for industry or government to ignore the years of training and experience of those who are over 40. I believe it is wrong that the impression should be given abroad, either by government or by industry, that a person is useless after 40. If that were true, there would not be many of us on the floor of the House of Commons, and there would not be any Senate at all. If that were true, the answer is that you must go where it is not true, namely in the Commons and the Senate, and there you can only find one vacancy in the House of Commons and 21 in the Senate. That procedure would not solve the problem at all. May I quote from a part of this editorial in the Southam press and may I say that I agree with it:
Only in jobs where straight muscle work is needed does the age factor play a big part. But in the machine age "muscle" jobs are not in the majority. This is an era for highly trained personnel, the technicians, mathematicians-skilled workers who can design machines or operate them.
Then it says this, Mr. Speaker, and with this I also agree because upon more than one occasion I have been approached by those under 40 and told this, "Why do you speak on behalf of those over 40? We young men need

The Address-Mr. Winch jobs". I think the Daily Province answers that question very well when in their editorial they said this:
This isn't a problem that concerns only those who are over 40. It concerns every Canadian, for young men and women who are now looking for their first jobs will one day be 40.
In the last paragraph the editorial also says this:
We hope the forties will be able to roar loud and long enough to bring this country to the realization that if it isn't willing to let these people work for their living it will have to pay for their keep in discontented idleness.
I am making these remarks, as I said, because I want to support the members of this house who spoke a few days ago in opposition to the government policy and the government lead to the effect that you are useless after you are 45 or after 40. I should like to add my words in support of the contention that this criticism also applies to industry. One's capability of work is not measured by his age: it is measured by his mental and physical condition. There are many men and women who are many years over 40; yes, there are quite a few of us right here in the House of Commons who, I hope, demonstrate that mentally and physically they have a contribution to make.
In conclusion I just want to say, on that one issue, that I sincerely hope it will not be necessary to have, as a complement to the provincial organization now started in Vancouver, a national organization to try to find jobs for those turned down by government and industry because they are over 40 years of age. If they were useless, the Acting Prime Minister (Mr. Howe) would not be sitting in his seat today. Our Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) would not be holding his job today. Ninety per cent of us would not be holding a job in the House of Commons. I hope the government will give some thought to this matter and will give a lead to industry. I hope they will give a lead to industry not only by the enunciation of policies but also by legislation such as some countries of the world have whereby there must be not only a percentage of those over 40 but those who are disabled in the employ of every employer.
I come now to my third point. It concerns a matter that has not been discussed in the house but I desire to raise it in this debate because I feel that it is of such importance that consideration should be given it by the government before they make a reply. I know that I could raise the matter when we come to the estimates but I should like a study made of it. While I was still in Vancouver before the house met I was interviewed by a number of men who were employed by the Canadian government on a

weather ship which operates off the coast of British Columbia. The ship is the C.G.S. St. Catharines.
Here, sir, is the consensus of opinion of experienced seamen on board that government ship. I was told that the policy with respect to the hiring of men on this weather ship operating off the coast of British Columbia is to engage men with no seagoing experience in preference to men with discharge books proving their ability and conduct at sea. I was told by those who interviewed me that promotion on this boat, at least in the deck department, is by favouritism without regard to experience and ability. I was told, and I am repeating only what I was told by those who met me, that cooks and waiters are constantly placed in seamen's berths and in an emergency would prove not only useless but even dangerous to other seamen and themselves. I was further told that proper types of life jackets for emergency boat work have been considered unnecessary by the local authorities although they were recommended by the master and the officers.
I was told by seamen on the boat that if a conscientious seaman found himself hampered by the type of life jacket supplied by the government in lifting a person or in pulling an oar he would be tempted to disregard the life jacket and endanger himself and others by taking it off. I was further told just before I came down here that all the personnel of the ship are concerned that the first aid facilities available on that weather ship are only of the most elementary nature, that on previous voyages cases of broken bones, acute appendicitis and severe eye injuries had occurred and the only treatment available was aspirin and laxatives.
These men made a recommendation which I want to pass on to the government. The recommendation was that they believed that a great improvement would be made if a fourth officer could be appointed on weather ships whose duties would not concern in any way the operation of the ship but who would give first aid training and proper boat and emergency training to enable the crew to deal with emergencies which might occur at any time during the operation of the ship.
I felt that this interview was important and that I should convey what was said to hon. members and to the government. Opponents of Social Credit have always endeavoured to show that it would establish a dictatorship. But quite the contrary is the case. The opponents of Social Credit will ask: "How could prices be maintained without iron controls?" By having and exercising ready, effective control over financial policy the minister of finance would be readily able to increase the supply of almost any commodity in Canada, thereby dealing with the tendency of prices to rise. Some will ask, "But how could he increase the supply quickly enough to offset an inflationary tendency?" On the other point, I do not think I can rule the hon. member out of order for reading quotations from a previous speech in this same debate, although I must say that there comes a time under the rules when lengthy reading of extracts is regarded as obstruction. At six o'clock the house took recess.
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, just before six o'clock the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) insinuated that I had made a speech in this house which someone had prepared for me. I think I should say that no one prepared my speech, nor do I think that anyone prepares the speeches of the hon. member for Lethbridge.

I am glad to hear the hon. member say that, Mr. Speaker.
Now, I was at the point of giving an account of the prosperity certificate to which the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) referred with complete propriety the other night. It is necessary to get the background of the whole situation in 1936 when the Alberta government attempted to issue prosperity certificates and use them.
In the first place, here are a few facts about Alberta's financial history. Alberta began her provincial existence in 1905 with no debt whatever. Between 1905 and 1921, under a Liberal government, she went into debt to the extent of $100 million. Up to 1935, under a U.F.A. administration following the 1921 election, she was in debt to the extent of $167 million. The average interest rate on that whole debt was 4.95 per cent.
Now, that was bad enough. Roughly $10 million of this $67 million debt which the U.F.A. had incurred, largely because of the depression, was in the form of Alberta savings certificates which represented money that had been borrowed by the government from ordinary people at 4 per cent. These Alberta savings certificates were provincial promises to pay on demand. This is exceedingly important to bear in mind. The total amount of that savings certificate debt was $9,414,468.15, to be exact. If hon. members are at all interested in facing facts they must recognize the significance of this $10 million worth of savings certificates, and the effect they would have on the credit of the province. Ask yourselves the question, what would you have done if you had been in charge of the province at that time, and then you will not feel nearly so smart when you are contemplating what Alberta did.
On August 27, 1935, the United Farmers of Alberta government had to announce it could no longer pay either interest or principal in respect of the savings certificates. This move destroyed the credit of the province. No longer could Alberta borrow money anywhere on the world's money markets; that is very important for all Liberals to bear in

mind. Social Credit had nothing to do with it at all. The Social Credit administration under William Aberhart's leadership took office on September 3, five days after the loss of Alberta's credit by the U.F.A.'s financial default.
What was the date of the election?

August 22; thank you for asking. Mr. Aberhart later said that when he became premier not only was the treasury empty but the bottom was scraped out of the barrel. My question is, what would you have done about it? What would the Liberal government have done if they had come to power at that time when the credit of the province was completely destroyed, with $10 million of demand savings certificates facing them, any one of which could be brought to their attention as a demand for payment at any time.
There were plenty of other difficulties, too.
In 1935 Alberta's economy was to a very large extent an agricultural economy and agricultural prices were tragically low. Freight rates were especially burdensome upon Alberta. Albertans were scarcely out of the very depths of the depression. To add to this adversity, in the year 1935, when Social Credit took over, Alberta's farmers in the south were afflicted with drought; in the north, they were rained out; in the centre, they were stricken with frost.
Oh, oh.

You notice the idiotic laughter which manifests itself every once in a while. It is an absolute refusal to face facts seriously.
The civil service had to be paid, and the other manifold obligations of a provincial government had to be met. I ask once more, what would a Liberal government have done in the circumstances? Answer that.
The Lethbridge Herald, in an article entitled "Watch Your Step", under date of August 21, 1935, the night before the election, used these words, and I quote:
We might as well be blunt about it and say positively and emphatically that if Alberta electors should send a majority of Social Crediters to Edmonton tomorrow, Alberta is headed for disaster.
Mr. Hoadley has told the people of Alberta that it is impossible for the province to finance itself through loans or bonds because of the fear investors have that Social Credit may come into control of the government of Alberta.
Alberta for the 18 months that Mr. Aberhart mentions wouldn't be able to finance itself. It could not make a loan; it could not borrow money, because the people who have the money wouldn't invest in a province where Social Credit was being experimented with. Then what would happen?
The Address-Mr. Blackmore
Aberhart could not administer the affairs of Alberta on the revenues that come to it from the people of Alberta only. Expenditures would have to be slashed, relief grants which up to the present have been financed mostly by loans from the Ottawa government would be cut down. So would mothers' allowance; old age pensions; hospital grants', school grants; all social and other services to which the people of Alberta have been accustomed.
Now, that was the sort of panicky talk that was taking place throughout the whole province.
The Social Credit government had promised improvement in every respect. There was an abundance of nearly every kind of goods and services. This is the important thing, Mr. Speaker. There were plenty of goods. It was said the warehouses were literally bulging with goods. There was a grave shortage of purchasing power in the hands of the people; that was all.
The province greatly needed roads everywhere. There were 80,000 miles of road allowances in Alberta, every mile of which needed good roads built along them. There were many thousands of unemployed in Alberta, all ready to go to work to build roads. There were many needy farmers who could work on roads while their crops grew or while they were waiting for another year's harvesting. There was plenty of road building material, such as gravel. There was sufficient machinery. There was food, clothing and shelter enough to sustain the workers. Is there any conceivable reason why the people of Alberta, roughly 900,000 of them should not have been able to work together to build these roads? Yet, under a Liberal administration those roads would never have been built at that time and would not be built today under similar circumstances.
The Social Credit government was a monetary reform government. The members knew that units of money created by a government could be sound if the units created were not too numerous in relation to the goods and services available. This had been abundantly proven through the operation of Canada's Finance Act of 1914, to which I referred on January 14. The dominion parliament had reaffirmed implicit confidence in the principles and performance of the Finance Act by extending that act in 1919 and then in reenacting it in 1923 as the Finance Act of 1923 under the great Liberal finance minister, Hon. W. S. Fielding. The reference to this is in the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada, published in 1933. In the face of these facts, why should not Alberta create money just as sound as the money created by Sir Thomas White, dominion finance minister? That is the first question.

The Address-Mr. Blackmore
In addition to the backing which Sir Thomas White would have, Alberta was placing a 100 per cent backing of coin and other Canadian cash in two years, to uphold these prosperity certificates. If Alberta affixed her signature to a million dollar bond, that bond was considered sound. Why should not a one dollar bond of Alberta be just as sound? When hon. members get that answer in a sensible manner, they will be in a position to appreciate the problem. The Alberta government, with obvious good logic, issued some thousands of Alberta one dollar bonds, called prosperity certificates. A million dollar Alberta bond to be redeemed in 20 years would be sound, why should not a one dollar Alberta bond to be redeemed in two years be sound? The prosperity certificate was in effect a bond and at the same time a promissory note. That was the status of the prosperity certificate; and all the laughing off by superficial minds will not change the situation one bit.
But any bond which might circulate-and here is where the difficulty arose-from hand to hand could be classified as currency. Here is where the stamp requirement entered the picture. Consequently if Alberta issued a one dollar bond and put it into circulation by trading it to an unemployed man in return for two hours of work on an Alberta road, then Alberta would be violating the currency legislation of the Dominion of Canada.
In order to avoid such dominion currency legislation Alberta had to penalize that road worker by obliging him, or whatever person accepted the bond from him, to put on the back of the bond a stamp from time to time, the denomination of the stamp being fixed at one cent and the period of time being fixed at one week. This was the only way that we could see of avoiding the currency law. It was not a question of whether the prosperity certificate was sound. It was a question of whether this big dominion government would permit the province to use that financial device in order to get out of what looked like an impossible financial situation.
The prosperity certificate was issued as a promise to pay by the provincial treasury.
I now refer hon. members to the passage which the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna) read into the record, which reading is accurate and which, as I said a few minutes ago, is a service to the country because it gives the people a chance to get the truth. If you get the full truth about Alberta there will be nothing but admiration and wonder as to how the administration ever got out of the difficulties they were in in 1935-all difficulties which they had nothing to do with causing-and all the time


being opposed by the most sordid opposition from the hon. members of the Liberal party, 100 per cent, all the time. Lies, misrepresentations and distortions just filled the air like smoke.
The date selected on which the stamp was to be affixed to the prosperity certificate, as I remember it, was Wednesday. Whoever found himself in possession of a one dollar prosperity certificate on Wednesday night at a certain hour would be required to affix to it a one-cent stamp. There was thus encouragement to people to keep the prosperity certificates circulating. The hon. member said that it looked like a giant taxation system. It could be looked at in that way. But look at the high degree of discount people will give right today in order to get a dollar's worth of trade. For almost any businessman today it would be an almost negligible thing to give one cent on the dollar to get a dollar's worth of trade, or any ordinary worker who is unemployed would certainly be glad to give one cent for the privilege of earning a dollar. That is what it amounted to.
The cause for the cessation of the use of these prosperity certificates was, of course, among other things, probably first the never-ending attack organized against them by the opposition. The very men whose party were responsible for putting Alberta in the financial position it was in were loudest, most inveterate and sordid in their opposition, trying to make it impossible for their own province to come out of the mire. There you have the record of the Liberals of 1935, and they are just as bad today. The last thing in the world they are ever concerned about is how the province is going to get ahead or how Canada is going to get ahead. The only thing that interests them is how to get their miserable selves back into office for another term.
The next reason was the fact that so many opponents of Social Credit refused to accept those prosperity certificates because of prejudice. There were many people who could just as well as not have accepted prosperity certificates such as people who were running stores, garages and the like. If they had accepted these certificates and passed them on just as they would any ordinary money, there would have been no burden on anybody and the effect would have been surprising on the prosperity and the pick-up generally of the province.
The third reason why prosperity certificates were not accepted was that they were not legal tender for obvious reasons. It was not the fact that the people as a whole rejected them. It was the fact that the stubborn, sordid Liberal opposition made it impossible for

the device to work. That is all it was. Let the blame go right where it should lie. They worked together with some Conservatives who were just as bitter as the Liberals were. What did they care about the well-being of their own province? Nothing!
I ask hon. members this question. How long would our present Bank of Canada dollars be accepted freely if in the first place a one-cent stamp were to be required to be affixed on the back of each dollar every week? There would be hesitation to accept it, would there not? But it would not be because the dollar is not sound. In the second place, if anyone in Canada were free to refuse to accept a Bank of Canada dollar in payment of a debt-that is if the dollar was no longer legal tender-how long would it be accepted? I think that is enough to show that it was not a matter of the prosperity certificate being unsound at all. Fundamentally, it was just as sound as any unit of money but it had to be used under these difficulties to which I referred in order to avoid the currency laws passed by this dominion parliament.
What were the accomplishments of the prosperity certificates? The hon. member did not tell us about those. I do not blame him. He was putting forward his own case. I will put forward mine. In the first place they built many miles of roads. Let it be borne in mind that when the Social Credit government of Alberta came into power there were only 75 miles of hard-surface roads in the whole province of Alberta. There were 80,000 miles of roads but only 75 miles of them were hard surfaced and that hard surface was the result of an experiment with the Athabasca tar sands and those hard-surface roads were not anything like what we call hard-surface roads today. Anybody who will go into Alberta today and travel over the magnificent system of highways to be found there will wonder how in the world any government of an agricultural province built that many fine roads in the course of 19 years. The prosperity certificates made possible the start. They helped to tide Alberta out of a financial position any other government would have found impossible.
I will say this. If a Liberal government had gone into power there, unless it had had a special dispensation from Ottawa or somewhere else, it could never have managed at all.
What might the prosperity certificates have done for Alberta if they could have been free from the handicap of stamps? The number of prosperity certificates that could
The Address-Mr. Blackmore have been issued and used in Alberta would have depended upon the surplus goods and services there were in Alberta ready for the people to buy and use, and that amount was simply stupendous. I do not know how many prosperity certificates could have been used but my opinion is that the government. could have issued enough of them until prices began to go up. Of course, the minute prices begin to go up, then you have inflation. That is the way to judge.
There are a great many people who say a great deal about the prosperity certificates, and who try to hold them up to ridicule and all that sort of thing. But that is not helping to solve the problems of this country. The Liberals today who are in power-the great big party with a tremendous majority -are just sitting like a lot of frozen tomato plants. They do not know what to do about this unemployment situation and they are trying to whistle in the dark to make themselves believe that the thing does not exist. But they just do not know what to do. Meanwhile their agents are at work misrepresenting Social Credit, the only thing that could help them solve the problem. I am sure I do not know what will happen if depression actually sets in. I am not saying that it will set in, but there is every indication that unemployment is going to increase. I ask the Liberals frankly: What are you going to do about this unemployment in case it continues to increase? Are you just going to sit like a lot of frozen tomatoes, waiting hopelessly just as your forebears did from 1935 to 1939-it is enough to make anyone just nauseated; it is a disgusting situation-while men tramped up and down and rode back and forth on the cars, almost hating the country in which they lived?
I ask: What harm did the prosperity certificates do to anyone? Did they ever cause inflation? No; no rise in prices. Was any one of them not redeemed? No; they were all redeemed in good Canadian money, except those that were not presented for redemption. The cost of the stamp was deducted but that is all. I ask once more: What would the Liberals have done? I should like to know what the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona, the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr Prudham) and the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Decore) would have done. I should like to have seen them form a government in the province of Alberta at that time and to have seen how they would have performed. These men are loud in their demands to destroy the government of the province of Alberta but just let them try to find a way out of the difficulties that faced Alberta then or that face Canada now.

The Address-Mr. Blackmore They would fail just as miserably as the Liberals failed in this house in 1935 to deal with unemployment and other ills in this country.
If the Liberals had gone into power in the province of Alberta of course they would *have gone for a loan. All they can think about is debt. They are never satisfied unless the country is loaded with an unbearable burden of debt. I think it was only five or six years ago that Harper Prowse, leader of the Liberal party in Alberta, said he would borrow $100 million and build a blanket of roads all over Alberta. That is exactly what he would do. He would have had the province loaded with such a burden of debt that every return it received from every source would have been required to service the debt. These Liberals would be perfectly happy to be able to wave helpless hands, shrug shoulders, and say they could not do anything about it.
If the Liberal organization had been in power there what would they have done? In those days the dominion government was talking about imposing a loan council upon the provinces which meant that in order for a province to obtain any amount of money beyond a certain figure it had to agree to allow the dominion government to tell it what it could or could not borrow. If Alberta had accepted a loan council in those days then her financial autonomy would have been destroyed. That is what the Liberals would have done. Meanwhile they would have left unemployed the people who were ordinarily employed on the roads through the use of prosperity certificates.
Just in passing I might ask the question: Why does the hon. member bring up the prosperity certificates here? I want to attribute nothing but the very best motives but it would be surprising if he did not bring up the prosperity certificates with the intention of trying to discredit the great Social Credit administration in the province of Alberta. The certificates were a trivial little thing that was only one of the struggles that the province made in its tremendous efforts to get out of the difficulties it was in.
Then I refer to the matter of dictatorship. It is an absolute falsehood to say that a Social Credit administration would have to have a dictatorship. If I do not know as much about it as the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Hanna), it would be a most astonishing situation. The statement that Social Crediters believe that printing money is all that is necessary in order to solve the difficulties of the country is just as false and preposterous as the other piece of nonsense.


I should like to give the house a picture of something on the happy side. What I have already given is a picture of the very unhappy situation which faced Alberta at that time. What is the situation of Alberta today as she faces this great fiftieth anniversary of her becoming a province? From a Canadian Press dispatch that appeared in the Lethbridge Herald of September 16, 1954, we learn that Alberta's net surplus for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1954, was $22,614,000. That is just about $9 million more than the total revenue Alberta had the first year after the Social Credit government took office in 1935.
In the year ended March 31, 1954, Alberta had revenues of $197,043,200, more than $42 million greater than the previous year. That is how this province of Alberta is growing today. Yet these Liberals would destroy the administration that accomplished that! How can they consider themselves to be patriotic Albertans?
Oh, oh.

If you will just listen you will learn something, but you do not learn if you do not listen. The government received from petroleum and natural gas leases $49,590,010. That is leases. The province of Alberta has reserved lands contiguous to parcels on which oil has been discovered, has held them until the time when people wished to have them and has sold the drilling rights on them on the open market at auction. During that one year the revenue from sales of such leases was $49,590,010. As I told some hon. members last year, if a Liberal government had been in power they would have had that money to divide among their friends.
The net funded debt of Alberta decreased in the year by $3,019,382. The unfunded debt of the province decreased by $83,304. Capital expenditure for the year was $89,911,864, including $35,228,877 spent on highways, bridges and ferries. There was $5,387,535 spent on public buildings and other public works, while $3,207,790 was spent on the St. Mary and Milk rivers irrigation project for capital development. The University of Alberta received $1,165,216 by way of capital expenditure. I wonder whether there is any reason why a government doing all that should be destroyed.
Loans and advances to municipalities and rural electrification associations amounted to $34,638,465 compared with $6,093,876 the previous year. The amount spent on public welfare, institutions and charitable grants was $36,453,388. Alberta's income from the federal-provincial tax agreement was $29,802,545. I am putting these last figures

on the record just so that we shall not have the Liberals running around telling people that the dominion government gave all the money to the province.
From the budget speech of the premier of Alberta delivered on March 5, 1954, we learn certain things about the debt situation of Alberta and I am going to give a series of figures so that we can see what has happened to the debt of Alberta since 1936 when the Social Credit government first began to manage the affairs of the province. As of March 31, 1936, the total debt was $167,027,144. In 1940 it was $156,501,773. In 1945 it was $150,159,819. All that happened before oil in any large measure was discovered. Oil was first discovered in great quantity in the Leduc field in 1947. As of March 31, 1950, the debt was $130,600,687. As of March 31, 1952, the debt was $100,437,090, and as of March 31, 1953, it was $97,452,424.
Table it.

And at December 31, 1953, it was $94,283,654. These figures show that there has been a very rapid decrease in the debt ever since the Social Credit administration took office. Not only were they able to pick up the reins and carry on by devices which they were able to work out, but they were able to reduce the debt from the very first year. Yet the Liberals in Alberta want to destroy the administration that has done that!

(Translation):

Mr. Speaker, may I first congratulate the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for the brilliant and courteous manner in which they have fulfilled their task.
I was not at all surprised at the oratory of the mover, the hon. member for Verdun, who has been for many years a fellow member of the Montreal bar.
I am sure that the movers of the address have expressed the feelings of their electors and that the latter have reason to congratulate themselves and to be proud of their members.
I take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, to congratulate the government on the efficient and worthy legislation already enacted and which they propose to enact during the session.
I represent an important Montreal constituency of approximately 100,000 people made up of Canadians of various racial origins, French, English, Jews, Poles, Italians and Ukrainians; all are unanimous in approving the way in which the government administers the affairs of the country.
The amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act have been well received by the public at large and they will alleviate the hardship of seasonal unemployment among a certain class of workers.
Some of the previous speakers have asserted that those amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act were but palliatives and would not remedy the situation. To refute their arguments one can say that there is and always will be seasonal unemployment, owing to the geographical position and the climate of our country.
I have been living in Montreal for over 30 years and every winter there has been a period of unemployment, more particularly among day labourers. Those people are happy today to be able to receive unemployment insurance benefits during that temporary period of unemployment; they consider this legislation beneficial and will find it even better following the amendments made by the government.

The Address-Mr. Meunier
It has also been stated in the house, Mr. Speaker, that the government's immigration policy was creating unemployment and depriving our workers of their livelihood. In the constituency of Papineau which I represent, there are many foreigners, the majority of which is made up of Italians. One must not believe that all these people come to Canada to seek employment and work as day labourers; many of them bring funds and go into business. In my constituency and elsewhere several of them have established marble, jewelry and watchmaking industries, and they employ Canadian labour without racial discrimination.
I have always found that the government's immigration policy was selective and that it did not increase the number of unemployed; on the contrary, it has helped Canadian industry to develop and expand. I am confident that the government will maintain that policy which is a source of stability for the Canadian economy.
The amendments which the government intends to introduce to the Blind Persons Act have been greeted with satisfaction by that group of citizens. A large number of blind people are finding it hard to make a living in spite of their talents and skills. They can hardly be expected to resort to begging. I feel confident that this government action will help lighten their burden and make their life somewhat more cheerful.
Another piece of social security legislation which was generally welcomed throughout the country was the Disabled Persons Act, passed by the house last year. This action by the government and especially by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), gained high praise everywhere. It will bring those people who come under the act valuable aid and comfort. These disabled people, who were a burden for others, will be able to bear their infirmity better, remembering that they are not forgotten. They will forget the difficulties of life and be in a position to procure relief and welfare for themselves.
Now, before closing, I wish to take exception to a remark made lately by one of the C.C.F. members in this house. The hon. member said that Quebec was the sore point with regard to national unity, that its people would react and that such reaction would be to the benefit of the communist party. I shall tell my hon. friend, the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier), that, if he has drawn such conclusions after visiting the province of Quebec, I wonder in what circles and in what places he has been. Yesterday the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin) gave him enough details on the life and

people of Quebec to make it unnecessary for me to go over it again.
The people of the province of Quebec are respectful of authority and of established order and I dare say to the hon. member that, if a very small group of the communist party stirs with no set purpose, the whole of the population cannot be made responsible for it. One has to live but a short time in the province of Quebec, as in any other province, to see that the people are in no wise different from the people of other provinces, but only that they have a Canadian mentality like the others and that they want the progress of the country, national unity and peace both in Canada and abroad.
We shall never see the day when the province of Quebec will be in the hands of the communist party, because the people of Quebec are too hardworking, sound and honest to believe in Utopia.
The people of Quebec are happy and content to live in a democracy and especially under the leadership of the Liberal party, which they have nearly always chosen to guide their political destiny.

Mr. Speaker, in common with many others who have preceded me in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne may I offer my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Leduc) and the seconder (Mr. Carrick), upon the fine manner in which they delivered their addresses. Their efforts were definitely worth while, and I was reminded of the occasion a few years ago when I had the opportunity of delivering my maiden speech in the House of Commons. With my own experience in mind, I believe I can sympathize with them in their ordeal.
Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring to your attention and to that of hon. members a simple and constructive step which can be taken immediately by the government to increase employment by at least 10 per cent in one of our most important industries, and at the same time save some Canadian consumers $71 million this year. I refer to a decision in the 1955 budget which would remove the excise or luxury taxes now levied on passenger automobiles.
I hasten to say that I am not advocating the removal of all taxes from automobiles. The present total of taxation amounts to 25 per cent of the manufacturer's selling price. Of this amount, 10 per cent is in the form of the general commodity sales tax, and the remaining 15 per cent is a luxury tax. It is this utterly unrealistic added burden of taxation on one of the most important and, I might add, most expensive necessities of

normal life under modern conditions in this country, which should be removed.
I am certain there is scarcely a member in the house who does not feel that this luxury tax should have been removed some years ago, when the reason for its imposition had ceased to exist. I refer of course to the fact that the automobile luxury tax, as we know it today, was first of all a wartime austerity measure and then a control device to conserve exchange and to combat inflation. It has been continued at its present or at a higher level for some years now, regardless of its depressing effect upon an industry which accounts for one-eighth of all retail sales, regardless of its limiting effects upon employment and regardless of the severe hardship it imposes upon consumers in the low and average income brackets.
The two great problems facing many Canadians today are unemployment and inadequate family income to meet the demands of our modern standard of living. The government could go a long way toward relieving both these problems if, in the forthcoming budget, it would abolish this outmoded and unrealistic luxury tax on passenger cars.
In some measure I speak of this growing need as a representative of the riding of Ontario, one of the two great centres of automobile manufacturing in Canada. I speak also in much larger measure for all Canadians who are forced to pay this arbitrary and artificial penalty of over $400 if they wish to buy the most modestly priced family car of Canadian manufacture on the market today. I admit that they should pay something, but I submit, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure all hon. members will agree, that $150 or $160 per car, which is the amount of the sales tax, is a fair contribution of this family necessity to the federal treasury.
The luxury tax costs each modest car owner an additional $240 or so. It is a luxury tax but in this case it is not imposed on the luxury. I think it will be generally agreed that this proposition is self-evident. The facts are-and this is the finding of a very thorough and extensive survey

that 83 per cent of passenger car use on an average day in Canada is for essential travel of one kind and another; that 65 per cent of every hundred miles of car travel is directly connected with the necessity of making a living; and that today almost one million of our citizens are driving, for these essential purposes, cars which are ten years old and more. Apart altogether from the important safety factors involved, it must be obvious that the continuance of this luxury penalty on new car ownership is seriously affecting the efficiency of the entire national productive effort.
The Address-Mr. Starr
The estimate I have given of a 10 per cent immediate increase in employment, if this luxury tax were removed, is conservative. Most labour leaders, I am told, think it would be considerably higher. Even so, I know what a 10 per cent increase in high pay employment would mean, not only in my own riding, or in the Windsor area, but in many other parts of Canada. Mr. Speaker, 260,000 Canadians depend for all or a large part of their income on the manufacture of motor vehicles, the supply of materials and component parts, and the sales and service of these vehicles. All would receive benefits, direct or indirect, from the removal of this luxury tax. Four thousand or perhaps five thousand new jobs would open up in the manufacturing industry alone and as many again in the supply industries. The latter, incidentally, actually give work to more people than the manufacturing industry itself.
I need not explain to this house, Mr. Speaker, that I am not talking about stopgap, marginal, low wage employment. The jobs I speak of are preferred jobs in our national work force. If our economy continues to expand, and the Canadian-made automobile is allowed its full share of the domestic market, they will be steady jobs.
It will give hon. members some idea of the magnitude of the burden of this present luxury tax on the payroll resources of the industry when I say that this year, and I mean the fiscal year 1954, the federal taxes paid by the automobile manufacturing industry in Canada exceeded the total paid in wages and salaries by some $13 million. The figures, I believe, are $137 million in taxes and $124 million in wages and salaries.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that on these facts alone, the immediate removal of the luxury tax would be fully justified. But there are other compelling reasons, perhaps the foremost of which is the long list of consumer benefits that would follow from the rechannelling of those $70 million into new disposable income. Some of it would be spent on cars, and much of it would be spent on other commodities. Regardless of what happened to it, the fact remains that Mr. and Mrs. Canada would have $70 million more in their pockets and purses, to spend or save, than last year.
If there is anybody on the opposite side of the house-and I am sure there is not one but many-who may be interested in raising the level of Canadian retail spending next year, I commend this simple and available source of substantial millions.
The exciting prospect of the immediate redistribution of these millions is even more
828	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Starr appealing if we look at the kind of Canadian families who will benefit the most. They are, naturally, the people who buy most of our passenger cars. Who are they? Again I quote the very reliable independent survey made of this and other basic facts of automobile ownership. Although it was made about three years ago, I am informed by those conversant with up-to-date statistics that its conclusions are still valid.
At the time of the survey, 81 of every 100 passenger cars were owned by households whose senior wage earner had an annual income of less than $4,000. Sixty-five of every hundred passenger cars were owned by families whose main source of income was less than $3,200. I have said that the luxury tax amounts to well over $200 in the cost of the average car. Its removal, Mr. Speaker, would be the equivalent of a round of pay raises of between 5 and 10 per cent for every $2,000 to $4,000 wage earner who buys a new car this year. I might say also at this point, sir, that I have inquired into the matter of passing on to the consumer the luxury tax removal, and I am most reliably informed that the entire reduction would be passed on by the manufacturers and dealers.
Also important in this connection-and I trust this aspect will have the serious consideration of the minister-is the application of the tax reduction or removal to cars in the hands of dealers. On some other occasions the government policy has been strangely inconsistent on this point. When the luxury or sales tax has been increased, this has generally been made to apply to all cars still in the hands of dealers. On the other hand, when reductions have been made it has not been applied to such cars. Perhaps I should explain that the sales and excise taxes on passenger cars are collected from the manufacturer before the car goes to the dealer for sale to the consumer. It is to all intents and purposes still an unsold car, merely having moved from the factory into the chain of distribution. Surely it is most unfair to all concerned to treat these cars still in the sales rooms and waiting to be sold as though they had actually been sold while the higher tax levels were in effect.
Of course, the tax will have already been paid on these cars by the manufacturer, and we all know how reluctant governments are to give back money to taxpayers, but surely the injustice of retaining such tax moneys is too obvious to allow this kind of thing ever to happen again. I have made some inquiries as to the practical aspects of giving these rebates, and am informed that the necessary checking, auditing and policing of dealers


is a simple matter which the large manufacturers could handle on behalf of the government without any untoward incidents.
As a matter of fact, Mr. Speaker, I will go so far today as to ask the Minister of Finance to make an immediate announcement that whenever new rates are announced, whether up or down, they will apply to all cars not actually sold to consumers. This is the only way to be absolutely fair. It might be thought that such an announcement at this time would suggest that a reduction or removal of the luxury tax had already been decided on. But this is not the case. Whether the tax is changed or not

and this could be acknowledged in the minister's statement-there will still be hesitation on the part of dealers to accept new car deliveries between now and the bringing down of the budget, unless such a policy is announced now.
It is common knowledge that there are rumours of some measure of automobile tax reduction in the air. I think it is not too much to say that the minister himself has had a good deal to do with starting those rumours. It would be a wise and gracious act on his part-and of immense help to the industry-if he would now recognize the difficult position of the dealers and state that no decision has been reached about next year's auto taxes-which is, I am sure, quite true-but that if or when changes are made, the new rates, up or down, will apply only when cars are sold to their new actual owners.
We must of course consider the effect of the tax removal on government revenues. I am sure that this is the question which is most important to the minister at the moment. I have said that the sum total of revenue from the luxury tax is currently about $71 million. However, even its complete removal would not mean a loss of anything like this amount to the treasury. I have heard various estimates of the actual loss, but the consensus of informed opinion is that it might be no more than half of the present tax "take", or about $35 million. This is due, of course, to the fact that the $71 million would go almost in its entirety into the main stream of consumer spending on cars and other commodities. The current estimate of the direct federal revenue on all commodity spending is between 20 and 25 per cent. That is one way the treasury would get back a substantial part of the $71 million. It would gain in other ways also.
For example, it would gain possibly 10,000 new taxpayers from the new jobs which the tax cut would create. Whether they came from other industries or not, the fact remains that new jobs would be created throughout

the economy, and we all know that new jobs mean inevitably new heads for the tax collector to count.
It would gain also from the substantial volume of new spending on cars, and from additional taxes on the accessories that always accompany new car ownership. The same applies to tires, car radios and so on, whose sales would be immediately stimulated by the upturn in new car buying.
I could mention many other general benefits from the measure of tax relief which I am advocating. It would afford some measure of relief to the overcrowded public transit systems of many of our cities. It would make life easier and simpler for those hundreds of thousands of Canadians who travel many miles to their work by passenger car, and to all of those who have fallen in with a new pattern of Canadian living, namely a small nome in the suburbs or countryside.
In closing, I am well aware that someone may ask the important question:	Why this
year? I think there are some compelling answers to that question. The sharp rise in unemployment is one current development that I am sure the government is anxious to check. I believe that the minister will find ready corroboration for the estimate of new jobs I have suggested, namely a 10 per cent rise in automotive manufacturing employment and at least an equivalent rise in the supply and service industries.
Another good reason for the tax cut this year is the fact, not generally realized, that one of the contributing factors to the economic slowdown of last year was a drop of 18 per cent in the total sales of the Canadian automobile manufacturing industry in 1954 over the previous year. I am told that the luxury tax removal would almost certainly restore that 18 per cent drop in the current year and then go on to add new production records to the output of this great industry in the years ahead.
I trust that I have said enough to make it clear, and to convince hon. members of the house, and particularly the government, that the 1955 budget is indeed the time for the final and long overdue removal of the luxury tax on this now common necessity.

Mr. Speaker, there has been considerable criticism regarding the excessive time occupied by the debate on the speech from the throne at the opening of each session. We should, however, remember that this debate is a report on the state of the nation. Each member of the house is given an opportunity to speak on the problems of his particular part of the dominion, and in that way parliament is given a survey of the problems and needs of the whole of Canada.
The Address-Mr. Schneider
Having been honoured by the privilege of seconding the motion in reply to the speech from the throne when I entered parliament, I can appreciate the excellent efforts by the mover (Mr. Leduc) and seconder (Mr. Carrick) this session. I wish to associate myself with all those who have congratulated them on their really fine speeches, and I feel that our parliament has gained two worthy members who will surely be an asset in our debates.
After a long and busy life in business, I am dismayed at the waste of time occupied by many speeches in the house and the needless quotations from newspapers and other writers giving opinions of very little interest to other members. We are elected to this parliament to express the opinions and the wishes of our constituents, but above all I believe that we are elected to act on our own decisions, and are personally responsible.
I am delighted that the throne speech calls for some revision of the house rules and I urge that private members' speeches be limited to 20 minutes. It has been estimated that the cost of operating parliament while in session is $10,000 a day. At this time we are sitting 5i hours per day, and that figures out to $1,818 per hour, and 20 minutes, which is one-third of that, cost $606. Surely no private member is vain enough to think that his ideas cannot be expressed in $606 worth of time, and that he should occupy $1,212 worth of time in 40 minutes.
The savings effected by this reduction would be fair to all and the party leaders' and ministers' privileges could remain as they are, giving ample time for summing up all the arguments presented without endless repetition by speaker after speaker.
Also the saving in the cost of printing of Hansard would be surprising when we think of the thousands of copies printed, and finally the printing and binding into those rows of big black books which gather dust in our offices.
A shortening of time of speeches would result in more time for the estimates at the end of the session and the real subject matter and purpose of the debate would benefit by a sharper focus resulting from the elimination of unnecessary repetition.
To faithfully represent the highly industrialized riding of Waterloo North, I must make a request regarding the excessive number of reports required from various departments of government. These federal reports added to all those from other levels of government represent a terrific amount of work in our business offices. Business is required to report the amount of various supplies and services used in the past year, and also estimate their requirements for the coming year.

The Address-Mr. Schneider How much, machinery, building construction, coal, fuel oil, and many other items require a great many reports? One company figures that they made out a total of 167 returns.
There is no denying the value of these statistics to some people, but I feel that as a rule the summary of it all is published so long after it is gathered that it is almost worthless. I urge the Department of Trade and Commerce, and particularly the bureau of statistics, to immediately give consideration to a study of the co-ordination of these government demands for information, and that all these questionnaires be looked at intelligently and sympathetically and some means be found to consolidate and minimize these reports.
The monthly coal statement is an example of their complaint. Coal was a problem during the war, but at present it is in good supply, and the same applies to fuel oil and many other items. In addition to the monthly reports we must also give a summary of the whole year, and woe unto the manager whose year's figures do not correspond with the monthly reports.
I have in my hand a resolution from the city council of Kitchener reading as follows:
That whereas the current unemployment situation in the city is a source of deep concern;
And whereas the Department of National Defence has already indicated their intention to construct an armouries in the city;
And whereas in the opinion of this council an armouries building in the city is greatly needed;
And whereas the building of a district income tax office has been proposed for this city;
Be it therefore resolved that this council petition the federal government to proceed immediately with the construction of these buildings as a means of alleviating in some measure the present unemployment.
There is also a letter from the Kitchener-Waterloo family service bureau board of directors drawing attention to the extent of the distress prevailing in our community because of the lack of some form of relief for the employable unemployed who have reached the end of their resources. The building of the new income tax office in Kitchener is assured, but the armouries is still a crying need in this hundred year old community with a combined population of over 70,000 in the twin cities of Kitchener-Waterloo. The patience and loyalty of our four units, the 54th light anti-aircraft regiment, the 48th field squadron, R.C.E.; the 3rd company, R.C.A.S.C., and the 24th field ambulance is commendable, and the oddity of an anti-aircraft regiment housed on the sixth floor of an office building does not help the militia.
I do not favour the idea of constructing public works projects for the purpose of relieving unemployment, but it would be of some assistance and would be justified in this


case. My deep concern is for the 3,479 unplaced applicants listed in the last report from our local unemployment insurance office. Many of the causes of the present business recession cannot be avoided during this painful readjustment to quick-changing world conditions. Canada took great pride in rapidly raising her standard of living, but now we find that we have priced ourselves almost out of the world markets. The only exception is the market of the United States, and they buy from us only when it suits them, and only until we interfere with their producers, at which time they protect them by raising the tariff or putting on an embargo.
Some of our hon. friends in the opposition seem to be extremely worried when Liberal members from industrial centres mention protection. We are labelled protectionist Liberals, but that does not worry us at all because we have the confidence of our constituents and throughout the years the Liberal government has always followed a policy of reasonable protection for our young and growing industries.
Hear, hear.

I am really amused by the criticism of opposition members, particularly the acting leader (Mr. Rowe), who feels that I am inconsistent and shed crocodile tears when pleading for protection for the factory workers of my riding. At first I was quite flattered by this attention from a veteran of 25 years in this parliament. I am no longer concerned about his misleading remarks, and have decided that his irritation is caused by the fact that in doing my duty I am doing what his non-conservative Conservative party should do according to policy and tradition.
You should be sitting over here.

I chose this seat.
During the last session there were as many good speeches for protection of the textile mills from this side of the house as there were from the Conservatives. The really outstanding speeches on behalf of the textile mills came from the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), on the Conservative benches, and the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. White) on the government benches. The Conservatives spent most of their time on the problem of wheat, hoping to gain favour in the west.
As the Acting Leader of the Opposition knows quite well, the percentage of Conservative voters in the cities in my riding is very high, almost 50 per cent. In criticizing me, does he suggest I should disregard their present plight and talk politics instead of

employment? I have chosen to place the interests of my people above party politics. The hon. member can follow his choice of politics first, but he cannot wisecrack me into following his ideas.
We have one convert, anyway.
Yes, a wisecracker. In the present recession-
The 20 minutes are up.

Oh, no. In the present recession, the problem has very seldom been insufficient protection. We have practically the same protection at this time as we had when conditions were considered to be at their best. In my opinion, the real causes of our problems today are the following: First, the dumping of surplus goods into our country in spite of Bill No. 29 passed during the last session, which makes provision for a price not lower than the average of the past six months in the country of origin. Secondly, the importation into our country of high grade goods and equipment which undersell our product in our home market because of the low wage rates in the country of origin. A good example of this is in the manufacture of electrical goods. The wages paid are as follows: Switzerland, 45 cents per hour; England, 53 cents; France, 58 cents; Belgium, 62 cents; Canada, $1.51 and the United States, $1.87. This comparison of rate is applicable to many importations into Canada today. In the face of this condition, how can we expect to sell in the export market?
Another cause of our unemployment is the serious loss of purchasing power of our farmers, both in the prairies and in the east. Farm income has dropped 15 per cent in the last two years, mostly as a result of lower prices for wheat. World wheat prices are definitely beyond our control, and along with all other wheat producing countries we suffered a drop of approximately 13 cents per bushel below the previous crop year. Because of the high cost of almost everything the farmer buys, he is having difficulty in making a profit on many of his products. The root of the problem is that while his selling prices appear to him to be low, these same prices have been amongst the highest in the world. According to last year's records the following wholesale prices prevail: beef in England, 21 cents; in Montreal, 33 cents; bacon in England, 28 cents; Montreal, 62 cents; cheese in England, 24 cents; Montreal, 32 cents; eggs in England, 50-6 cents per dozen; Montreal, 52-4 cents. The problem is to find some way to market our surplus abroad at prices which will give the producer a fair return. Experience has
The Address-Mr. Schneider proven that when the farmer is prosperous he spends his money on equipment made in the city and we are all prosperous.
Another serious cause of unemployment, and one which is particularly irritating to our Canadian manufacturers, is the unsympathetic attitude of some of our government purchasing officials. Directives have been given to all such officials by the various ministers, but we still find orders and contracts for foreign made equipment being given when a Canadian company could supply it, sometimes at a lower price. Orders are sometimes given to Canadian companies who in turn buy and supply foreign goods. It is an unpleasant experience to lose such an order to a foreign firm, pay taxes to pay for the goods and send your employees home for lack of work. I appeal to all government spending bodies to carefully check each and every purchase to make sure that all possible employment is given to Canadian workmen.
Hear, hear.
It is easy to stand here and say what you think is wrong with our country, but it is quite another matter to offer a solution to these problems.
Hear, hear.
Who is making this speech, please?
It sounds like a Conservative.
It is your own members in the rump over there who are interrupting.

It is easy to stand here and say what you think is wrong with our country, but it is quite another matter to offer a solution to these problems. Our young country could be compared to a young boy at his first birthday party. Johnny Canuck is a lively youngster with a reputation as a hearty eater and a fast grower. Other people outside his family have great confidence in him and are urging him to eat everything in sight. They are killing him with kindness by feeding him operating capital for investment in this wonderful country faster than he can digest it. Foreign capital has been fed into Johnny Canuck so fast that his dollar value has a premium of 3i per cent over the dollar of the richest country in the world, namely the United States of America. This diet is too rich for his stomach and while this high dollar value feels good at first, it is just like Johnny's cake and ice cream, and now he has an old-fashioned bellyache. Our high dollar value of 1.034 is a serious handicap in selling our surplus products in the export market. If our 3 A per cent premium were removed we

The Address-Mr. Bryce would gain an advantage of approximately 6 cents per bushel on our export sales of wheat. That would result in a faster movement of our surplus wheat and would greatly relieve Johnny Canuck's stomach ache.
Our dollar at par, or lower, would immediately stimulate our export trade and it would discourage the spending of our Canadian shopping and vacation dollar in the United States with whom we are so far out of balance.
Very few of us have training or experience in international finance, and I am sure I do not know how this devaluation of the Canadian dollar can be accomplished. But unpleasant as, it is, many Canadians agree that it is one of the solutions for the present problem. While I certainly do not advocate or compare our present position with that of Great Britain, I believe that they devalued the pound sterling to about half of its former or normal value. Surely if they did it our financiers can also find a way to give us some relief.
Great Britain is enjoying full employment while we sit here with Johnny Canuck's stomach full of rich food and like all small boys he does not want to take his castor oil. This parliament should encourage our finance minister in his present efforts to find some solution to this most pressing problem and to give us at least an even break with the United States dollar in securing export trade.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened attentively to the hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Schneider) and what he had to say with regard to what it costs when one rises to speak for 10, 15 or 20 minutes in the house. I have been trying to figure how much it is going to cost for me to speak for this 5 minutes. However, I am not going to allow a little thing like that to worry me, because this is something that has been going on since 1867 and it will not be changed in my time. I want to draw something to the attention of the government and I am not going to take long about it. I have never before spoken twice in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Many letters are arriving at our desks these days asking what the government intends to do regarding support prices on the various agricultural commodities. I want to take this opportunity of bringing this very important matter before the house at this time.
Canadian farmers have shown a strong preference for stability in the prices they receive for their products as against the wide price fluctuations that result from the operation of the so-called free market. Undoubtedly the majority, like industrial workers, prefer a reasonable, assured income to a "feast-or-famine" arrangement.

At the end of world war II, in 1944, the Agricultural Prices Support Act was passed "to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture" and "to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations". The act was continued until 1950 when it was made permanent legislation.
In practice, the act has done little to provide the farmer with a stable income but has rather been used in times of emergency, such as the 1952 foot-and-mouth disease outbreak, to ward off some of the effects of the drastic reduction in the farmers' earnings. Also, the three-man prices support board set up under the act has done little or nothing to keep farm income under review and take steps to carry out the terms of the act. This board was established to examine the need for support for various commodities from time to time. The act laid down no conditions for support and no methods for determining the extent of support. Each commodity is treated as a special case. In practice the board acts only when approached by a group of producers, or in a widely recognized emergency. At no time has a formula been set up that people would understand. When a price has been set, it seems to have been something that someone reached up in the air for and said, "That is it". There should be a formula based on the cost of production and some return for the producer, and it should be something that would apply to all the different cases. The board can only recommend, since the cabinet decides what support, if any, shall be given.
Support may apply throughout certain periods to all or to only a limited quantity of a commodity which is produced in certain areas. It may be given by offers to purchase or by guarantee of price. In 1944 a fund of $200 million was allowed, or set aside with losses to be recovered from the consolidated fund each year.
By far the greatest expenditures-about 85 per cent from 1944 to March 31, 1954- have been those made for hogs and cattle as a result of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease.
Most support has been short-term. Butter is the only commodity for which support prices have been announced for two year periods, but even then the announcement has been made just before the beginning of the period.
That the board deals most frequently with wholesalers and packers rather than directly with farmers has provoked strong criticism in the country. Prices are negotiated with the wholesalers and packers so that they

will be able to pay, with some profit to themselves, certain prices to producers. It has been said that farmers have received as little as 10 cents a dozen for eggs for which packers received 38 cents plus 5 cents for storage. Instances were cited in the House of Commons here of producers obtaining from $1 to $2 less in Winnipeg, and from $3 to $4 less in Saskatoon than they were entitled to per hundredweight of beef. Even when the full price has been allowed it has often not covered the farmers' costs, with the result that production was drastically reduced in the following season. In 1950 potato growers in the maritimes planted 105,000 acres of potatoes. The next year their price was supported at only $1.20 per barrel and acreage was reduced by 35 per cent. Consumers in Toronto had to pay 66 cents for 10 pounds of potatoes in January, 1952.
In its brief to the cabinet in 1953 the Canadian Federation of Agriculture stated:
The announcement of the reduction in the floor price for hogs from 26 cents to 23 cents apparently resulted in a very serious reduction in sow breedings. . . . We believe that in the best interest of more stable production and price, it would be advisable to establish a higher floor than 23 cents in order that production might be maintained iu future months at least at the level of domestic requirements.
Because of the low support price production dropped, and pork loin sold in Toronto in January, 1954, at 78 cents per pound.
Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, if my hon. friend were not reading his speech he could not get so far away from the facts as he has been ever since he started.
That is not a point of order.
Mr. Speaker, I take credit for being a better reader than some of the members on the other side of the house.
Some of the others stick to the truth.
That is all right.
